The Brain Creates Body Ownership Before Touch Occurs

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (966 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers have mapped the exact millisecond-by-millisecond sequence of brain activity that creates the feeling that a hand belongs to our own body.
  • Recent findings suggest that we effortlessly take for granted that our hands, arms, and limbs belong to us.
  • While prior neuroimaging studies identified the general brain regions involved in self-perception, the exact temporal choreography, when each region activates and how signals cascade across the cortex, has remained elusive.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers have mapped the exact millisecond-by-millisecond sequence of brain activity that creates the feeling that a hand belongs to our own body. The magnetoencephalography (MEG) study reveals three distinct neural phases, beginning even before physical touch occurs, and explains why right-hemisphere strokes frequently cause patients to disown their left arm.

Recent findings suggest that we effortlessly take for granted that our hands, arms, and limbs belong to us. Yet this seamless sense of body ownership is an active perceptual construction, one that requires the brain to continuously merge visual, tactile, and spatial signals in real time, and one that can shatter dramatically following neurological injury.

While prior neuroimaging studies identified the general brain regions involved in self-perception, the exact temporal choreography, when each region activates and how signals cascade across the cortex, has remained elusive.

Now, in a study published in Nature Communications, neuroscientists at Karolinska Institutet led by Professor Henrik Ehrsson (Department of Neuroscience) and co-author Professor Daniel Lundqvist (Department of Clinical Neuroscience) have charted the birth of body ownership millisecond by millisecond.

To capture how the brain constructs the feeling that a limb is its own, the team recruited 45 healthy volunteers for a precision robotic version of the classic rubber hand illusion.

It has been revealed that participants watched a lifelike artificial hand resting in front of them while their real left hand remained hidden behind a screen. Two robotic arms delivered brief, synchronized touches to both the visible rubber hand and the concealed real hand, while high-speed magnetoencephalography (MEG) recorded whole-brain magnetic fields. By comparing synchronized touches (which trigger the illusion that the rubber hand is part of one’s body) against asynchronous touches and real-hand control conditions, the researchers isolated the neural signature of body ownership across the 28 participants who vividly experienced the illusion.

Reconstructing brain activity every four milliseconds produced a real-time movie of self-perception unfolding across three distinct phases:.

Recent findings suggest that “We know quite a lot about which areas of the brain are involved in the sense that the body is our own, but considerably less about when different areas become active and how they interact. We have now been able to track how activity patterns in the brain develop over time,” explained Ehrsson.

“The fact that the activity began even before the hand was touched reveals that the brain’s expectations of what we are going to feel are closely linked to the conscious experience of the body as our own,” added Lundqvist. “This study shows when, in what order, and how different brain regions help combine information from different senses into a unified experience of our own body.”.

Notably, during the first two phases of the sequence, neural activity was confined almost entirely to the right hemisphere. This lateralized timing aligns strikingly with clinical neurology: following a stroke, patients who experience somatoparaphrenia, the disturbing condition in which a limb no longer feels like part of one’s own body, almost always disown their left arm after damage to the right hemisphere.

It has been revealed that “When stroke patients lose the sense that an arm belongs to them, it is usually the left arm that is affected, following damage to the right hemisphere of the brain,” Ehrsson noted. “In future studies, we want to compare patterns of brain activity associated with the right and left hands to better understand the different roles of the brain’s hemispheres. We also want to collaborate with stroke researchers to investigate this phenomenon in patients.”.

How does the brain create the feeling that your hand belongs to your body?

In a recent development, karolinska Institutet researchers found that body ownership arises through a precise three-stage sequence of brain activity. It starts with predictive expectation before a hand is even touched, sweeps rapidly across the right frontal, parietal, and cerebellar regions, and finally engages the left hemisphere to unify sensory information.

Why did brain activity start before the hand was physically touched?

It has been revealed that seeing an object approach the hand triggers predictive brain activity based on what we expect to feel. This pre-touch expectation primes the brain to merge sight and touch into the conscious experience that the limb is our own.

How does this study help explain disturbed body perception after a stroke?

Because the first two critical stages of body ownership occur almost exclusively in the brain’s right hemisphere, damage to that side from a stroke disrupts the early multisensory integration needed to recognize the left arm, explaining why stroke patients frequently lose the sense that their left arm belongs to them.

Industry observers note that funding: The study was funded by the Swedish Research Council, the Göran Gustafsson Foundation, the Torsten Söderberg Foundation and the Swedish Brain Foundation. NatMEG receives support from the Knut and Alice Wallenberg Foundation. The researchers declare no conflicts of interest.

Spatiotemporal brain dynamics of limb ownership perception.

We experience our limbs as our own, but how does the brain generate this fundamental sense of body ownership?

Previous studies have relied mainly on fMRI or lesion mapping, providing a static view of the neural mechanisms underlying body ownership.

Using magnetoencephalography, robotically controlled visuotactile stimulation, and multivariate analysis across the rubber hand illusion, a real hand condition, and multiple control conditions, we identified source vector dissimilarity patterns reflecting ownership of the left arm.

Three phases of ownership-specific activity patterns emerged: (i) anticipatory patterns in medial frontal cortex, right posterior parietal cortex, and right posterior cerebellum before tactile stimulation; (ii) multisensory integration patterns in right dorsal and ventral premotor cortex, right posterior parietal cortex, and anterior cerebellum at 116–156 ms poststimulus; and (iii) later bilateral insular and left hemisphere patterns at 184–232 ms.

These findings provide a whole-brain, time-resolved map of activity patterns underlying body ownership, revealing its dynamic neural construction.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that how do major collectors use social media to help them navigate the art world? The latest Art Basel & UBS Survey of Global Collecting 2026 report, which surveyed 3,100 high net-worth individuals (HNWIs) who collect art, shows that social media platforms—and Instagram in particular—are an increasingly important tool for discovering art and artists, buying works and promoting collections. Here is how online platforms are being used and what the art world can learn from it.

Recent findings suggest that while the most common routes into collecting according to the report were the influence of family (28% of respondents) and cultural exposure through visits to museums, galleries, and fairs (22%), a surprising 13% discovered art collecting independently through online channels or social media. Interestingly, online channels were a less common route into collecting for Gen Z collectors (10%) than for Gen X (16%), “running against any assumption that younger collectors might be more likely to find their way to collecting through digital channels”, the report notes.

According to recent reports, the data also shows that those who started their art collecting journey online had higher levels of engagement with in-person exhibitions and events, both locally and overseas. “While being introduced to art through family or cultural exposure may reflect a more passive route into collecting, those who started out online were typically more active in seeking out art content,” the report indicates. “This suggests a more deliberate, self-directed collecting journey that carries forward into greater engagement with events later on.”.

When it comes to collecting, 58% of respondents remarked they had used digital resources for advice with 32% of collectors citing either Instagram or X (formerly Twitter) as sources when it came to making purchases. Nineteen percent used recommendations from Instagram (up 2% year-on-year), including 22% of Gen Z respondents, and women were more likely to use them than men. The platform X—which has seen decreased usage in recent years due to controversies around its ownership and usage—was used by 18% of the sample, and this was again highest among Gen Z (23%).

A collectors’ likeliness to use social media recommendations for collecting also depended greatly on where a person was from: collectors in Hong Kong, the US and the UK were most likely to use social media for advice while those in Mainland China were less likely, undoubtedly due to the restrictions of social media platforms in the country.

Contrary to popular belief around the slow uptake of artificial intelligence (AI) in the art world, the study also indicated that collectors trusted AI tools for art recommendations twice as much as those from social media and influencers, and also slightly more than in-store advisors and editorial content.

According to recent reports, the importance of ​​online and social media platforms in reaching collectors is growing. According to the survey, 27% of HNWIs’ total expenditure was made through such external platforms, up by 5 percentage points year-on-year and from 17% in 2024. The share of collectors buying directly from artists also grew to 69%, with 38% of works bought via Instagram, highlighting the benefits of a strong, independent social media presence for artists. It is also interesting to note that artist-direct spending through Instagram was higher among fresh collectors than more experienced ones: 8% for those in the market for two years or less, versus just 2% for those collecting for 20 years or more.

But can seeing a work online really seal the deal? Apparently so—among the 75% of respondents who had purchased a work directly from a dealer in 2025/2026, 53% had bought via Instagram without viewing the work in person, up from 43% in 2024.

Recent findings suggest that the report interestingly states that the youngest generation of collectors—Gen Z—are not the ones using social media the most in their collecting journeys. “The generation raised on social media is, it turns out, the one most inclined to keep its collecting close,” the report claims. While the data showed that Gen Z were the highest-spending generation surveyed and had the most wide-ranging collecting habits, their awareness of digital footprints leads them to seek greater control and privacy over their "personal and cultural identities".

Sources indicate that “Anonymous accounts and smaller, niche social networking platforms allow them to communicate in ways that feel less pressurised and performative,” the report states. “With social media feeds heavily controlled and populated by algorithms rather than personal networks, Gen Z consumers are increasingly interested in taking back control over who sees their personal content by sharing it with smaller, vetted and carefully chosen audiences.”.

When it came to sharing information about their collections with the wider public, only 25% Gen Z shared their own content publicly, compared with 36% of millennials and around one third of other older collectors.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sometimes what we see does not immediately make sense.
  • In a study published in Nature Neuroscience, Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory Cynthia R.
  • The findings offer a possible explanation for how the brain combines information from specialized regions into a single, coherent perception.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sometimes what we see does not immediately make sense. A shadow can briefly resemble a face, or one object can momentarily be mistaken for another. New research suggests that the brain may resolve these visual conflicts by allowing different regions to compare their interpretations until a more consistent picture emerges.

In a study published in Nature Neuroscience, Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory Cynthia R. Stebbins Fellow Mitra Javadzadeh and collaborators at the University of Cambridge and University College London examined how two neighboring regions of the visual cortex interact. They found that when activity in the two regions matched, the shared pattern persisted. When the regions produced conflicting patterns, however, the disagreement faded within a fraction of a second.

The findings offer a possible explanation for how the brain combines information from specialized regions into a single, coherent perception.

How Specialized Brain Regions Work Together.

Sources indicate that different parts of the brain are responsible for processing different streams of sensory information, yet our experience of the world usually feels unified rather than fragmented. Understanding how those specialized systems coordinate with one another is a major challenge in neuroscience.

"We are trying to understand how you can have such a high level of specialization between these different blocks, yet always have a consistent holistic outcome," Javadzadeh notes.

The researchers focused on two well known visual processing regions in the brain's neocortex: the primary visual cortex (V1) and the lateromedial visual area (LM). Visual processing does not simply move in one direction from one region to the next. Instead, these areas continually exchange information with each other.

Testing What Happens When Visual Areas Disagree.

Recent findings suggest that to explore that communication, Javadzadeh and her colleagues trained mice to tell the difference between two visual patterns tilted in opposite directions. The animals received a reward for recognizing only one of the orientations.

Industry observers note that during the task, the researchers temporarily silenced either V1 or LM and watched how the remaining region behaved without its usual partner. The team then used those observations to create an artificial neural network model of the V1-LM circuit. With that model, they could test how the system might respond when particular neurons were altered.

In a recent development, the results revealed a striking pattern. Activity that conflicted between the two brain regions quickly disappeared, while activity shared by both areas lasted longer.

"We find that over time, these types of connections between areas implement a mechanism we call consensus building," Javadzadeh explains.

A Possible Brainwide Consensus Mechanism.

The study examined only two regions involved in vision, but the researchers are now investigating whether the same process may operate more broadly across the neocortex.

"For example, when what you see contradicts with what you hear, do you still use the same kind of mechanisms to reconcile these two?" she wonders.

Sources indicate that if dynamic consensus building turns out to be widespread, it could help scientists better understand how the brain combines competing signals into a stable interpretation of the world. It could also shed light on what happens when different brain regions fail to arrive at the same conclusion.

The idea may even have implications beyond neuroscience. Similar principles could help researchers think about how artificial intelligence systems might handle conflicting streams of information and decide which signals to trust.

"While we understand individual building blocks of the brain, what is the glue that puts them together?" Javadzadeh asks. "Knowing that can finally help us understand how the brain works as a whole.".

💡 Key Takeaways

  • For the roughly one in five Americans living with a mental health condition, frontline psychiatric medications have changed remarkably little since the 1950s.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that fresh neuroscience research reveals that both psilocybin and ketamine improve decision accuracy by helping the brain rely less on rigid, repetitive habits and more on real-time sensory cues. The study highlights that rather than scrambling neural signaling, these compounds gently sculpt ongoing brain activity, trading a slight reduction in reaction speed for sharper, more flexible choices.

For the roughly one in five Americans living with a mental health condition, frontline psychiatric medications have changed remarkably little since the 1950s. Conventional antidepressants such as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) often require weeks to take effect, demand chronic daily use, and fail to provide adequate relief for roughly 30% of patients with treatment-resistant depression.

In a recent development, against this backdrop, psychedelic compounds, including classic serotonergic psychedelics like psilocybin and dissociative agents like ketamine, have sparked intense clinical excitement for their ability to produce rapid, durable improvements in mood, addiction, and post-traumatic stress disorder. Yet precisely how these drugs alter neural circuits to break entrenched patterns of negative thinking has remained poorly understood.

Now, in a study published in Science Advances, neuroscientists at Boston University led by assistant professor Dr. Benjamin Scott and associate professor Dr. Steve Ramirez have uncovered a shared pro-cognitive mechanism linking psilocybin and ketamine: both drugs weaken the brain’s reliance on automatic habits and heighten sensitivity to immediate sensory cues.

To test how psychedelics influence moment-to-moment decision-making, Scott, Ramirez, and colleagues trained mice on a perceptual task requiring the animals to use brief pulses of light to identify which of two ports contained a reward.

It has been revealed that untreated mice performed the task moderately well, but frequently fell into habitual traps—repeatedly returning to a previously rewarded location even when the light cues clearly signaled a change. Following administration of either psilocybin or ketamine, however, mice made significantly fewer errors. Rather than falling back on repetitive choice biases, treated animals anchored their decisions much more closely to real-time sensory information.

“These findings reveal how psychedelics reduce the reliance on habits and repetitive choices, which may explain part of their therapeutic effect,” explained Scott, a faculty member in Boston University’s Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences.

Although psilocybin acts primarily on serotonin receptors (such as 5-HT2A and 5-HT1A) while ketamine blocks glutamate NMDA receptors, their behavioral effects converged on sharper, less biased decision-making.

To observe what changed inside the brain, the researchers combined brain-wide genetic activity mapping with targeted neural recordings in the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), a prefrontal region essential for evaluating rewards, making decisions, and updating beliefs when rules change.

Remarkably, psilocybin did not erase or scramble existing task representations. Instead, core OFC activity patterns tracking sensory cues and choices remained largely intact, accompanied by widespread yet subtle adjustments across interconnected brain regions. According to the authors, this gentle sculpting of ongoing neural activity aligns closely with clinical observations that a person’s mindset and environment (“set and setting”) strongly shape the psychedelic experience.

According to recent reports, the team also identified an important behavioral nuance: while mice made more accurate choices after receiving psilocybin or ketamine, they took longer to deliberate, revealing a classic speed-accuracy tradeoff. While slower deliberation can benefit reflective cognitive therapy, it underscores why activities demanding split-second reaction times, such as driving, are unsafe under the influence of these compounds.

Looking ahead, Scott and Ramirez proposal to pinpoint the exact neural pathways responsible for breaking rigid habits, with the ultimate goal of developing targeted, next-generation therapies that unlock cognitive flexibility without hallucinogenic side effects.

How do psilocybin and ketamine improve decision-making in this study?

Boston University researchers found that both drugs help the brain pay closer attention to immediate sensory cues (like flashes of light) while reducing the tendency to fall back on repetitive habits, leading to significantly more accurate choices.

Do psychedelics scramble normal brain activity during a task?

Industry observers note that no. Recordings in the orbitofrontal cortex demonstrated that the brain’s core patterns for tracking cues and making decisions remained largely preserved. Instead of causing chaos, psilocybin induced widespread yet subtle shifts that gently sculpted how the brain updated its beliefs.

Were there any downsides to the improved decision accuracy?

Sources indicate that yes. Researchers observed a speed-accuracy tradeoff: while treated animals made fewer mistakes, they took longer to make their decisions, suggesting these compounds slow down reaction times even as they promote more deliberative thinking.

Psychedelics Shift Decision Strategies and Reconfigure Orbitofrontal Dynamics.

Psychedelics such as psilocybin and ketamine are attracting renewed attention as rapid-acting therapeutics, yet how they reshape cognitive computations remains poorly understood.

To address this, we trained mice on a free-response perceptual decision-making task that disentangles bias-driven from sensory-guided strategies. Acute administration of psilocybin or ketamine slowed decision times while improving accuracy. Behavioral modeling combining drift diffusion and GLM-HMM approaches revealed that these effects were driven by increased decision thresholds and a shift toward sensory-engaged states.

It has been revealed that whole-brain c-Fos mapping identified modulation of distributed task-related networks, including the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC). Calcium imaging indicated that OFC population dynamics were reorganized under psychedelic conditions, with preserved task selectivity but altered temporal structure and shifted population correlations.

Together, these findings indicate that psychedelics shift decision-making toward greater reliance on sensory evidence while reshaping cortical population dynamics, providing a system-level account of their effects on perceptual decisions.

Scientists just discovered what coffee really does to your gut and brain

📅 28 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (939 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Coffee may affect far more than alertness.
  • Scientists at APC Microbiome Ireland, a research center at University College Cork, investigated in detail how coffee may influence communication between the digestive system and the brain.
  • The study published in Nature Communications and sponsored by the Institute for Scientific Information on Coffee (ISIC), found that both caffeinated and decaffeinated coffee were associated with changes in the gut microbiome as well as differences in mood and stress.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Coffee may affect far more than alertness. New research suggests that both regular and decaffeinated coffee can alter the gut microbiome and may influence mood, stress, memory, and attention through the gut brain connection.

Scientists at APC Microbiome Ireland, a research center at University College Cork, investigated in detail how coffee may influence communication between the digestive system and the brain.

The study published in Nature Communications and sponsored by the Institute for Scientific Information on Coffee (ISIC), found that both caffeinated and decaffeinated coffee were associated with changes in the gut microbiome as well as differences in mood and stress.

How Coffee May Affect the Gut-Brain Connection.

Scientists have long studied coffee for possible effects on digestion, mood, and overall health, but exactly how these effects arise has remained less clear.

The fresh research focused on the microbiota-gut-brain axis, the two-way communication system linking microorganisms in the digestive tract with the brain. Signals can travel between the gut and brain through immune activity, hormones, nerves, and chemical compounds produced by microbes.

According to recent reports, researchers examined 31 regular coffee drinkers and 31 people who did not normally drink coffee. Participants completed psychological assessments and kept records of caffeine intake and diet. Researchers also collected stool and urine samples to track changes in gut microbes, metabolism, mood, and perceived stress.

For the study, 'Coffee drinkers' were set as those who regularly consume 3-5 cups of coffee a day, defined by the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) as a safe and moderate amount for most people.

What Happened When Coffee Was Removed.

Industry observers note that the regular coffee drinkers first stopped consuming coffee for two weeks. During that period, participants repeatedly completed psychological assessments and provided stool and urine samples.

When coffee drinkers stopped drinking coffee, researchers observed substantial shifts in their gut metabolite profiles compared with people who did not normally consume coffee. Metabolites are small molecules produced or altered during metabolism, including compounds created by gut microbes as they process food and other substances.

Coffee was then reintroduced without participants knowing whether they were receiving caffeinated or decaffeinated coffee. Half received decaf, while the other half received caffeinated coffee.

It has been revealed that after coffee returned to their diets, both groups reported lower perceived stress, depression and impulsivity scores. The findings suggest that some of coffee's effects on mood may not depend entirely on caffeine.

Coffee Was Linked to Changes in Gut Bacteria.

Researchers also found differences in several types of gut bacteria.

Bacteria, such as 'Eggertella sp.' or 'Cryptobacterium curtum', were more abundant among coffee drinkers than non-coffee drinkers. 'Eggertella sp' is thought to contribute to acid secretion in the stomach and intestines, while 'Cryptobacterium curtum' may participate in bile acid production.

Both processes could potentially help create an intestinal environment that discourages certain harmful bacteria and infections.

Researchers also observed higher levels of 'Firmicutes' bacteria, a broad group of microbes that has previously been associated with positive emotions in females.

Decaf and Caffeinated Coffee Showed Different Effects.

One of the most intriguing findings was that caffeinated and decaffeinated coffee did not appear to affect participants in exactly the same way.

It has been revealed that improved learning and memory were observed only among participants drinking decaffeinated coffee. That finding suggests that substances other than caffeine may contribute to some of coffee's effects on cognition.

Recent findings suggest that coffee contains thousands of chemical compounds, including polyphenols. These plant derived substances can act as antioxidants and can also interact with gut microbes, potentially influencing metabolism and other biological processes.

Caffeinated coffee, meanwhile, was associated with reduced feelings of anxiety as well as improved vigilance and attention. Caffeine was also linked to a reduced risk of inflammation.

Because the study involved a relatively small number of participants, the findings do not establish that coffee directly causes these changes in mood, cognition, or gut health. However, they provide new clues about the biological pathways that could help explain associations reported in earlier coffee research.

In a recent development, corresponding author of the study, Professor John Cryan, Principal Investigator at APC Microbiome Ireland, University College Cork, commented: "Public interest in gut health has risen hugely. The relationship between digestive and mental health is also increasingly being better understood, but the mechanisms behind coffee's effects on this gut-brain axis have remained unclear.

Industry observers note that "Our findings reveal the microbiome and neurological responses to coffee, as well as their potential long-term benefits for a healthier microbiome. Coffee may modify what microbes do collectively, and what metabolites they use. As the public continues to think about dietary changes for the right digestive balance, coffee has the potential to also be harnessed as a further intervention as part of a healthy balanced diet.".

Sources indicate that the findings add to growing evidence that coffee should not be viewed simply as a source of caffeine. Its many other components may interact with the microbiome, metabolism, and nervous system in different ways.

According to recent reports, "Coffee is more than just caffeine -- it's a complex dietary factor that interacts with our gut microbes, our metabolism, and even our emotional well-being," said Professor Cryan. "Our findings suggest that coffee, whether caffeinated or decaffeinated, can influence health in distinct but complementary ways.".

Rising Blood Sugar in Young Adults Hurts Midlife Brain Health

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (983 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A 30-year longitudinal study reveals that young adults whose fasting blood sugar gradually rises over decades face significantly worse cognitive health by midlife, even if they never develop Type 2 diabetes.
  • While Type 2 diabetes has long been recognized as a risk factor for late-life dementia, cognitive impairment linked to blood sugar was historically thought to emerge primarily after age 65.
  • Now, a three-decade investigation published today in the Journal of the American Heart Association demonstrates that creeping elevations in fasting blood sugar starting in young adulthood can measurably undermine memory, processing speed, and executive function by middle age, even among individuals who never cross the diagnostic threshold into full-blown diabetes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A 30-year longitudinal study reveals that young adults whose fasting blood sugar gradually rises over decades face significantly worse cognitive health by midlife, even if they never develop Type 2 diabetes. Tracking nearly 3,000 adults from age 18 into their mid-50s, researchers found lower memory, processing speed, and executive function scores among those with rising glucose trajectories, alongside structural brain changes in participants who developed Type 2 diabetes.

Source: American Heart Association.

While Type 2 diabetes has long been recognized as a risk factor for late-life dementia, cognitive impairment linked to blood sugar was historically thought to emerge primarily after age 65.

Now, a three-decade investigation published today in the Journal of the American Heart Association demonstrates that creeping elevations in fasting blood sugar starting in young adulthood can measurably undermine memory, processing speed, and executive function by middle age, even among individuals who never cross the diagnostic threshold into full-blown diabetes.

Led by first author Dr. Regina Paradela (postdoctoral researcher at the University of São Paulo Medical School and neuroepidemiologist at the Global Brain Health Institute at UC San Francisco) and senior author Dr. Kristine Yaffe (director of the Center for Population Brain Health at UC San Francisco), the study tracked metabolic and cognitive trajectories across 2,808 participants in the landmark Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults (CARDIA) cohort.

Enrolled between 1985 and 1986 at ages 18 to 30 across four U.S. cities, participants underwent repeated fasting blood glucose measurements over 30 years until reaching an average age of 55. At the 30-year mark, all participants completed comprehensive neuropsychological testing, and a subset of 605 participants underwent brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).

By mapping longitudinal glucose patterns across the 2,463 participants who remained free of Type 2 diabetes, the researchers identified three distinct metabolic trajectories:.

An additional 345 participants developed Type 2 diabetes (fasting glucose ≥126 mg/dL) during the 30-year follow-up.

Even after adjusting for demographic and lifestyle factors, both the increasing-glucose group and the Type 2 diabetes group performed significantly worse on tests of memory, processing speed, executive function, and global cognition compared with the lower-stable glucose group.

“The fact that increasing glucose levels were associated with poorer cognitive performance, even among people who had not developed Type 2 diabetes during the 30-year study, is very crucial,” explained Paradela. “This suggests that changes in glucose metabolism may be relevant to brain health earlier in adulthood than we typically think about.”.

Furthermore, MRI scans revealed tangible anatomical footprints among participants who developed Type 2 diabetes, who exhibited less total gray matter and more abnormal white matter tissue, markers closely tied to accelerated brain aging and cognitive decline.

“Future research should evaluate whether monitoring and managing increasing glucose levels earlier in adulthood can prevent or delay cognitive decline and structural brain changes,” mentioned senior author Yaffe.

Commenting on the study, Dr. Elisabeth Marsh, professor of neurology at The Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine and chair of the writing group for the American Heart Association’s 2026 scientific statement Brain Health Across the Life Span, emphasized the value of early vascular and metabolic care: “The American Heart Association’s Life’s Essential 8 offers steps to improve heart and brain health and support cognitive well-being at every stage of life.”.

Can rising blood sugar harm brain health even if you don’t have diabetes?

Yes. Over a 30-year study, young adults whose fasting blood sugar gradually increased into the prediabetic range (110–115 mg/dL) scored significantly worse on midlife tests of memory, processing speed, and executive function than peers whose blood sugar remained low and stable, even though they never developed Type 2 diabetes.

What structural brain changes were seen in participants who developed Type 2 diabetes?

MRI brain scans revealed that adults who developed Type 2 diabetes by their mid-50s had less total gray matter volume and more abnormal white matter tissue compared to those who maintained lower-stable blood sugar levels from young adulthood.

When should adults start paying attention to blood sugar for brain protection?

Researchers note that changes in glucose metabolism begin affecting cognitive performance much earlier than age 65. Monitoring and managing blood sugar trajectories starting in young adulthood, using healthy nutrition, physical activity, and cardiovascular risk control, may help protect midlife and late-life brain health.

Funding: Co-authors, disclosures and funding sources are listed in the manuscript.

Trajectories of Fasting Blood Glucose and Brain Health in Middle Age.

Research on associations between long‐term fasting blood glucose (FBG) trajectories and brain health in early adulthood is limited. We investigated associations of FBG trajectories with cognition and brain structure.

According to recent reports, participants were from the CARDIA (Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults) study, followed for 30 years, who completed ≥1 cognitive test at year 30. Among participants without diabetes with ≥3 FBG measurements from baseline to year 30, we identified FBG trajectories using latent growth mixture models. Participants who developed diabetes after baseline were included for comparison (n=345). Cognition was assessed using tests of processing speed, executive function, memory, fluency, and global cognition. Structural magnetic resonance imaging data from 605 participants included total gray matter volume and white matter lesions. Associations were examined using multivariable linear regression adjusted for demographics and health behaviors.

Sources indicate that we included 2808 participants (mean age, 55.2±3.6 years; 56% women; 44% Black individuals). Three FBG trajectories were identified: lower‐stable (n=1387), moderate‐stable (n=938), and increasing (n=138). Compared with the lower‐stable group, increasing FBG and incident diabetes were associated with worse performance in memory, processing speed, executive function, and composite cognition; increasing FBG was also associated with worse global cognition. Incident diabetes was associated with lower total and parietal gray matter volume and greater parietal white matter abnormalities. No consistent sex or race interactions were observed.

Persistently elevated glucose below the diabetes threshold was associated with worse cognitive performance in midlife, while incident diabetes was associated with structural brain changes.

Tech Report: Why Nerve Pain Lingers

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (897 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers uncovered a molecular pathway in the spinal cord that drives persistent neuropathic pain long after an initial nerve injury.
  • Source: Guizhou University of Traditional Chinese Medicine.
  • In a recent development, for millions of people living with neuropathic pain, even a feather-light touch or a mild shift in temperature can ignite excruciating discomfort long after an initial physical injury has healed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers uncovered a molecular pathway in the spinal cord that drives persistent neuropathic pain long after an initial nerve injury. The multi-omics and electrophysiological study reveals that nerve injury suppresses the nuclear regulatory protein Nono, triggering a steep drop in Kcnq2 potassium channels that normally calm spinal pain neurons, while restoring Nono reverses pain hypersensitivity in animal models.

Source: Guizhou University of Traditional Chinese Medicine.

In a recent development, for millions of people living with neuropathic pain, even a feather-light touch or a mild shift in temperature can ignite excruciating discomfort long after an initial physical injury has healed. Rather than stemming solely from ongoing tissue damage at the original wound site, persistent nerve pain is frequently driven by central sensitization, a state in which pain-processing circuits inside the spinal cord become hyperexcitable and amplify ordinary sensory signals.

Now, a comprehensive study published in Research by scientists at Guizhou University of Traditional Chinese Medicine, Fudan University, and partner institutions has pinpointed a critical molecular switch behind this spinal hyperexcitability: the Nono–Kcnq2 regulatory axis.

By combining five layers of molecular profiling with single-neuron electrophysiology and behavioral testing, the team demonstrated how nerve injury silences a vital genetic brake inside spinal neurons—and revealed that restoring this pathway alleviates chronic pain sensitivity.

Under healthy conditions, neurons in the spinal cord’s dorsal horn rely on specialized potassium channels to stabilize their electrical charge and prevent runaway firing. When potassium ions flow out of a neuron, they keep excitability in check; when those channels disappear, neurons fire rapidly in response to minimal stimulation.

It has been revealed that to trace why potassium channel control breaks down after nerve trauma, the investigators examined a rat model of chronic sciatic nerve constriction, which produces pronounced mechanical and thermal pain sensitivity within three days. Electrophysiological recordings confirmed that spinal dorsal horn neurons fired far more readily while exhibiting sharply diminished outward potassium currents.

Applying an integrated multi-omics pipeline, spanning proteomics, phosphoproteomics, transcription factor profiling, spatial transcriptomics, and single-cell RNA sequencing across 48,279 spinal cord cells, the researchers mapped the exact cellular shifts occurring at seven and 21 days post-injury:.

Sources indicate that molecular binding experiments confirmed that Nono directly binds to a conserved region of the Kcnq2 gene promoter to drive its expression. To test whether repairing this broken link could relieve pain, the researchers delivered an adenoviral vector carrying Nono into the spinal region of nerve-injured rats.

Increasing Nono expression successfully rebuilt Kcnq2 protein abundance, restored protective outward potassium currents in dorsal horn neurons, and significantly eased mechanical and thermal pain hypersensitivity. When the team applied XE991, a selective pharmacological blocker of Kcnq2/3 potassium channels, both the restored potassium currents and the behavioral pain relief were largely reversed, confirming that Nono alleviates pain specifically by reactivating Kcnq2 channels.

While the researchers emphasize that clinical therapies remain a long-term goal—noting that experiments were conducted in male rats and that additional pathways also contribute to neuropathic pain—the findings illuminate a clear mechanistic bridge linking gene transcription to electrical excitability in the spinal cord.

Rather than merely masking pain signals with broad analgesics, future therapies aimed at preserving Nono activity or supporting Kcnq2 potassium channel function could help quiet overactive spinal circuits at their molecular source.

Why can neuropathic pain persist even after a nerve injury has healed?

Following nerve trauma, neurons in the spinal cord can undergo central sensitization, becoming abnormally excitable so that they amplify harmless signals like light touch or mild warmth into intense pain.

What did researchers discover about the Nono and Kcnq2 proteins in the spinal cord?

Scientists found that nerve injury reduces the activity of the nuclear protein Nono, which normally switches on the Kcnq2 gene. Kcnq2 produces potassium channels that act like electrical brakes to calm spinal neurons; when Kcnq2 levels drop by up to 80%, pain neurons fire excessively.

Did restoring Nono reduce pain sensitivity in the animal study?

Yes. When researchers used a viral vector to restore Nono expression in the spinal cord of rats with nerve injuries, Kcnq2 potassium channel levels rebounded, neuronal firing calmed down, and the animals highlighted significantly less sensitivity to mechanical and thermal pain.

Multi-Omics Analysis Reveals Nono–Kcnq2 Regulation of Neuronal Excitability in Chronic Constriction Injury-Induced Neuropathic Pain.

Recent findings suggest that neuropathic pain, resulting from somatosensory nervous system damage or disease, is a debilitating condition marked by spontaneous pain, hypersensitivity, and sensory abnormalities. Neuropathic pain involves spinal neuronal hyperexcitability, yet its molecular basis remains poorly defined.

We utilized a comprehensive multi-omics approach, incorporating proteomics, phosphoproteomics, concatenated tandem array of consensus transcription response elements, and both single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, to chart time-resolved adaptations in the L4 to L6 spinal cord of a chronic constriction injury rat model.

Multi-omics revealed remodeling of glutamatergic synapse pathways and identified non-POU (Pit-Oct-Unc) domain-containing octamer binding (Nono) as a down-regulated transcription factor associated with reduced potassium voltage-gated channel subfamily Q member 2 (Kcnq2) expression. Nono and Kcnq2 were co-enriched in neurexin 3-positive and peripherin-positive spinal neurons.

According to recent reports, restoring Nono expression up-regulated Kcnq2, enhanced K+ outward currents (an effect largely abolished by the Kcnq2/3 blocker XE991), and alleviated pain hypersensitivity. Mechanistically, Nono was enriched at a conserved Kcnq2 promoter region in vivo and enhanced Kcnq2 promoter activity in reporter assays.

Together, these findings established a Nono–Kcnq2 transcriptional axis that constrained spinal excitability and suggested a therapeutic entry point for neuropathic pain.

#173475. Children at risk for depression get “stuck” on sad faces

General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Children at risk for depression get “stuck” on sad faces

📅 29 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (883 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A smile or a frown may reveal more than emotion alone.
  • New research from Binghamton University, State University of New York, suggests that depression may influence how strongly children focus on emotional expressions such as happy or sad faces.
  • According to recent reports, researchers at the Mood Disorders Institute at Binghamton University study how depression develops in children and adolescents, with particular attention to how family history and emotional experiences may influence vulnerability over time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A smile or a frown may reveal more than emotion alone. The faces that capture a child's attention could provide crucial clues about their mental health and how depression develops.

New research from Binghamton University, State University of New York, suggests that depression may influence how strongly children focus on emotional expressions such as happy or sad faces. The pattern appears to differ depending on whether a child has a family history of depression.

According to recent reports, researchers at the Mood Disorders Institute at Binghamton University study how depression develops in children and adolescents, with particular attention to how family history and emotional experiences may influence vulnerability over time. By identifying these patterns while children are still developing, scientists hope to better understand who may be at greater risk and eventually improve prevention strategies.

"Most of the vulnerabilities that we focus on are still developing during this time period," noted Brandon Gibb, director of the Mood Disorders Institute and SUNY distinguished professor of psychology. "You can catch things as they're developing, rather than only studying them once they're already there and pretty stable.".

Following Children's Attention Over Time.

Earlier research has linked depression with greater attention to sad faces. However, those associations have generally been modest, and scientists have not been sure whether biased attention contributes to depression or develops because of it.

Sources indicate that the Binghamton study was designed to investigate that question by tracking both depressive symptoms and attention patterns over time. According to the researchers, it is the first study to examine how changes in each may predict later changes in the other among children.

It has been revealed that "The real novel piece is that we looked at these transactional relations," remarked Kelly Gair, a PhD student at Binghamton and lead author of the paper. "Between attentional biases and depressive symptoms, we looked at the way that they were mutually predicting one another across the time points, which is especially novel and hasn't been done before.".

The research team, which also included Leslie A. Brick from the University of Latest Mexico, followed 242 children and their mothers for two years. Participants were assessed every six months.

During each visit, children viewed pairs of faces on a screen. One face revealed a neutral expression, while the other displayed an emotion (happy, sad, or angry). Eye tracking technology measured which face held the child's attention and for how long.

Children in the study looked at faces conveying different emotions onscreen, and eye tracking technology recorded where their attention veered. Photo credit: NimStim Set of Facial Expressions (Tottenham et al., 2009).

Family History Changes the Pattern.

Sources indicate that the results suggest that increasing depressive symptoms do not affect every child's attention in the same way. Family history appeared to play an notable role.

Among children whose mothers had a history of major depressive disorder, rising depressive symptoms were associated with greater attention to sad faces. In other words, as these children experienced more symptoms themselves, their attention became increasingly drawn toward expressions of sadness.

"For those who are already at risk, the more these children experience depression themselves, the more they lose their ability to pull their attention away from the sad things around them," Gibb mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that "We know that when you're depressed, it changes what you pay attention to," Gair noted. "Our results suggest that these changes may be more long-lasting and may differ depending on family history. One thought is that for children of mothers with depression, who are exposed to more facial displays of sadness from interactions with their mom, these types of facial expressions become even more salient when they experience depression themselves, so their attention becomes increasingly stuck on sad expressions.".

Happy Faces May Lose Their Pull.

A different pattern emerged among children whose mothers had no history of depression.

When depressive symptoms increased in these children, they did not become more focused on sad expressions. Instead, they paid less attention to happy faces.

"In our lower-risk children, what seems to be happening is that experiences of depression are eroding a protective factor, which is how much they pay attention to happy faces," Gibb said.

The distinction suggests that depression may alter emotional attention through different pathways depending on a child's underlying level of familial risk. For some children, sadness may become increasingly difficult to ignore. For others, positive emotional signals may simply become less likely to capture their attention.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers are continuing to follow the children as they enter adolescence, a period when the risk of developing depression increases for many young people. They hope to determine whether these early attention patterns are associated with a greater likelihood of receiving a depression diagnosis later on.

The paper, "Transactional Relations Between Attentional Biases for Affective Stimuli and Depressive Symptoms in Offspring of Mothers With and Without Major Depressive Disorder," was published in the Journal of Psychopathology and Clinical Science.

Adolescent Brain Circuits Shape Lifelong Social Drive

💡 Key Takeaways
  • New research reveals that adolescence is a critical developmental window for a brain pathway linking the prefrontal cortex to the ventral striatum (PFC-vSTR).
  • Recent findings suggest that adolescence is widely recognized as a period of intense behavioral and social transformation, marked by heightened peer seeking, shifting relationships, and emotional turbulence.
  • Now, latest findings from The Ohio State University Department of Psychology pinpoint a critical developmental window inside a pathway linking the brain’s executive command center to its reward hub: the prefrontal cortex–ventral striatum (PFC-vSTR) circuit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

New research reveals that adolescence is a critical developmental window for a brain pathway linking the prefrontal cortex to the ventral striatum (PFC-vSTR). The study demonstrates that temporarily quieting this reward-and-motivation circuit during adolescence leads to lasting social withdrawal in adulthood, shedding light on why psychiatric conditions like depression and schizophrenia often emerge during the teenage years.

Source: The Ohio State University.

Recent findings suggest that adolescence is widely recognized as a period of intense behavioral and social transformation, marked by heightened peer seeking, shifting relationships, and emotional turbulence. While neuroscientists have mapped early infant brain development in granular detail, the exact neural mechanisms sculpting social behavior during the teenage years remain far less understood.

Now, latest findings from The Ohio State University Department of Psychology pinpoint a critical developmental window inside a pathway linking the brain’s executive command center to its reward hub: the prefrontal cortex–ventral striatum (PFC-vSTR) circuit.

Sources indicate that presented at Neuroscience 2026, the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience, by lead author and doctoral candidate Katrina Lin alongside senior investigator Dr. Laurence Coutellier, the study demonstrates that disrupting PFC-vSTR maturation during adolescence permanently dampens adult social motivation.

To establish how social drive naturally evolves across the lifespan, Lin and Coutellier first measured spontaneous social investigation in both adolescent and adult mice, whose compressed three-week adolescent window enables researchers to trace developmental trajectories across adulthood.

According to recent reports, “I always say it’s like two dogs in a park. They start sniffing each other. They’re careful at first, and then they go into a different type of sniffing behavior,” explained Coutellier, associate professor of behavioral neuroscience at Ohio State. As predicted, adolescent mice exhibited substantially higher motivation to initiate social interaction than adult mice.

Sources indicate that “In humans it’s the same,” Coutellier noted. “A teenager loves to hang out with their friends, and they will seek this interaction. As adults, we will be more careful. We don’t approach a stranger just like that, and we’ll be more cautious about the way we interact. There’s still a strong social motivation, which is necessary for us to have social relationships, but there is less of it.”.

The prefrontal cortex, which governs decision-making, impulse control, and social reasoning, and does not finish maturing in humans until roughly age 25, sends direct signals to the ventral striatum, a core hub for reward processing and motivation.

To test whether adolescent maturation of this pathway is essential for adult sociability, the team selectively switched off activity in PFC-vSTR neurons in both male and female mice during either adolescence or adulthood:.

“We found that actually, yes, if we prevent the maturation of the frontal circuit to the striatum, when mice reach adulthood they have impaired social motivation,” Coutellier noted.

Understanding how the PFC-vSTR pathway wires itself during adolescence carries significant implications for psychiatry. Conditions such as depression and schizophrenia frequently manifest during the teenage years, often preceded or accompanied by profound social withdrawal.

Next, Coutellier’s laboratory plans to examine how real-world environmental stressors, such as prolonged adolescent social isolation, alter the maturation of this circuit.

Industry observers note that “We can try to study what happens when our mice don’t get to socialize, and we can think about what happened during COVID-19, when teenagers were told to stay home and stop socializing to be safe. How did that impact this developmental trajectory of the social circuits?” Coutellier asked. “We’re trying to understand what genetic and environmental factors can make these symptoms arise at the time of adolescence — not before, and not in adulthood, but during that sensitive period of development.”.

What is the PFC-vSTR brain circuit, and what does it do?

In a recent development, the prefrontal cortex–ventral striatum (PFC-vSTR) circuit connects the prefrontal cortex (the brain’s decision-making and social control center) to the ventral striatum (a key hub for reward and motivation). During adolescence, this pathway matures to support healthy social motivation and peer interaction.

Why did turning off this pathway in teenage mice affect them as adults, while adult mice bounced back?

Sources indicate that researchers found that adolescence is a uniquely sensitive developmental window when this circuit is still actively wiring itself. Disrupting it during adolescence permanently altered how the circuit matured, leading to reduced social motivation in adulthood, whereas adult brains already have established wiring that recovered immediately once the inhibition ended.

How does this research relate to mental health conditions like depression and schizophrenia?

Recent findings suggest that many psychiatric disorders first appear during the teenage years and involve social withdrawal. Identifying the exact brain circuits that mature during adolescence helps scientists understand how genetic risks or environmental stressors, such as social isolation, can derail healthy social development.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • People with dementia, mild cognitive impairment, alcohol addiction, and psychiatric conditions such as schizophrenia may show signs of accelerated brain aging, according to a study published in the open access journal PLOS Medicine.
  • In a recent development, researchers can estimate whether a person's brain appears older or younger than expected for their chronological age.
  • According to recent reports, to investigate how different brain conditions might influence this measure, the researchers analyzed structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data from 45,900 controls drawn from several brain imaging databases.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

People with dementia, mild cognitive impairment, alcohol addiction, and psychiatric conditions such as schizophrenia may show signs of accelerated brain aging, according to a study published in the open access journal PLOS Medicine. The research, led by Shile Qi of the Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics, China, found that different conditions appear to be associated with distinct patterns of aging across the brain.

In a recent development, researchers can estimate whether a person's brain appears older or younger than expected for their chronological age. One way to do this is with predictive age difference (PAD), which compares a person's actual age with an age estimated from brain imaging. A positive PAD means the brain appears older than would typically be expected.

According to recent reports, to investigate how different brain conditions might influence this measure, the researchers analyzed structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data from 45,900 controls drawn from several brain imaging databases. They compared those scans with data from 2,698 people with a range of conditions and differences, including attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), autism spectrum disorder (ASD), alcohol or tobacco addiction, Alzheimer's disease (AD), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), schizophrenia, bipolar disorder or major depressive disorder.

Alzheimer's and MCI Show the Strongest Associations.

Among the conditions examined, the neurodegenerative disorders AD and MCI highlighted the strongest associations with higher PAD values, suggesting the greatest degree of accelerated brain aging.

Addiction and psychiatric disorders were also associated with increased PAD. By contrast, the researchers found no overall differences in PAD between controls and people with ADHD or ASD.

Different Disorders Affect Different Brain Regions.

The team also examined PAD across individual brain regions and looked at patterns of gene expression associated with the different conditions.

It has been revealed that one area that stood out was the prefrontal cortex, which showed higher PAD across multiple brain disorders. Psychiatric disorders were associated with elevated PAD in the frontal and temporal lobes, while dementia was linked to higher PAD in the frontal and occipital cortex.

Recent findings suggest that addiction showed a different pattern. Higher PAD was observed in the default mode network, as well as in the salience network, putamen and thalamus.

The researchers also identified differences in gene transcription associated with particular conditions and divergences, suggesting that the patterns of brain aging may be linked to distinct underlying biological processes.

A Potential Source of Future Biomarkers.

The findings do not show that these conditions directly cause accelerated brain aging. The study is correlational, and some conditions, particularly psychiatric disorders and addiction, frequently occur together, which can make their individual effects difficult to separate.

Even so, the researchers suggest that studying PAD more closely could eventually help identify biomarkers associated with common brain disorders and provide new clues about the biological pathways involved.

The authors add, "Different neurological disorders appear to leave different signatures on the brain aging clock, which may help researchers better understand the neural and biological pathways involved in these conditions.".

The funders had no role in study design, data collection and analysis, decision to publish, or preparation of the manuscript.

Brain Predicts Spoken Mandarin Differently Than English

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • New neuroimaging research reveals that the human brain uses a distinct predictive strategy when listening to spoken Mandarin compared to Indo-European languages.
  • To keep pace with the rapid flow of natural conversation, the human brain does not simply wait passively for words to arrive.
  • Industry observers note that until now, however, most neurobiological models of predictive speech processing have been built almost exclusively on studies of English and other Indo-European languages.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

New neuroimaging research reveals that the human brain uses a distinct predictive strategy when listening to spoken Mandarin compared to Indo-European languages. The study reveals that while Mandarin listeners simultaneously track phonemes, sub-syllables, characters, and words, predictive brain signals occur primarily at the sub-syllabic level, where lexical tone integrates with speech sounds, rather than at the level of individual phonemes.

To keep pace with the rapid flow of natural conversation, the human brain does not simply wait passively for words to arrive. Instead, auditory and language circuits continuously forecast upcoming sounds, syllables, and words, generating neural “surprise” signals whenever spoken input deviates from expectation.

Industry observers note that until now, however, most neurobiological models of predictive speech processing have been built almost exclusively on studies of English and other Indo-European languages. How the brain anticipates speech in tonal, logographic-linked languages such as Mandarin Chinese, where pitch contours alter word meaning and syllables serve as tightly unified building blocks, has remained far less explored.

In a study published in eNeuro, researcher Qifei Wang and colleagues at Radboud University investigated how the unique structural and tonal architecture of Mandarin shapes real-time neural predictions during naturalistic listening.

To capture the brain in action during continuous speech comprehension, the research team recorded neural activity from 34 native Mandarin speakers as they listened to an audiobook.

By modeling the acoustic and linguistic properties of the story alongside the participants’ brain responses, the investigators discovered that neural activity simultaneously tracked multiple nested units of spoken Mandarin:.

Next, the team analyzed how strongly the brain anticipated incoming speech at each linguistic level by measuring neural responses to expected versus surprising sounds.

According to recent reports, in a striking departure from prior findings in Indo-European languages, the researchers detected no clear evidence of predictive neural signaling at the individual phoneme level in Mandarin. Instead, predictive effects stood out most strongly at the sub-syllabic level, where lexical tone contributed significantly when integrated with other speech-sound features.

This divergence highlights how the brain adapts its computational strategy to match the structural rules of a speaker’s language: whereas Indo-European listeners rely heavily on fine-grained phoneme transitions to forecast words, Mandarin listeners anchor their predictions to larger, tone-integrated sub-syllabic units.

By demonstrating that understanding Mandarin relies on parallel, multi-level linguistic predictions centered on tone-integrated sub-syllables rather than isolated phonemes, the study underscores the importance of linguistic diversity in cognitive neuroscience, showing that universal models of human language must account for how different writing and tonal systems organize speech inside the brain.

How does the brain keep up with fast spoken conversation?

Rather than passively waiting to hear every sound, the brain actively predicts upcoming speech elements based on context. When incoming speech is surprising or unexpected, the brain generates distinct neural responses that help upgrade comprehension in real time.

How does processing spoken Mandarin differ from English and European languages?

According to recent reports, in English and other Indo-European languages, the brain strongly predicts speech at the level of individual sounds (phonemes). In Mandarin, Radboud University researchers found no clear predictive effects at the phoneme level; instead, the brain makes its strongest predictions at the sub-syllabic level, where pitch tone combines with speech sounds.

What units of speech did the brain track while listening to a Mandarin audiobook?

Brain recordings from 34 native Mandarin speakers demonstrated that the brain simultaneously tracks four nested layers of spoken Mandarin at once: individual phonemes, sub-syllables, characters, and full words.

Neural Signatures of Predictive Processing During Natural Mandarin Speech Comprehension.

It has been revealed that language comprehension requires the continuous transformation of speech into a hierarchy of linguistic units, from phonemes to syllables to words. Because speech unfolds rapidly, listeners are thought to predict upcoming content to keep pace. Previous research has provided empirical evidence for predictive processes operating at multiple linguistic levels during naturalistic listening, including words and phonemes. However, it remains unclear whether prediction also operates concurrently at other levels, such as syllabic and phrasal representation.

In a recent development, here we use Mandarin Chinese to examine the neural signatures of predictive processing across multiple levels of linguistic granularity during natural speech comprehension. Mandarin comprises four representational levels: phoneme, sub-syllabic, character and word, and its lexical identity is largely constrained at the sub-syllabic level, potentially redistributing predictive weight across linguistic representations.

It has been revealed that we recorded magnetoencephalography (MEG) data while 34 native Mandarin speakers (21 females) listened to a naturalistic audiobook and applied linear regression modeling to examine how linguistic features modulated neural activity. We found that the brain activity of listeners segmented speech into hierarchical units, and that surprisal modulated responses simultaneously across sub-syllabic, character and word levels.

Recent findings suggest that in contrast to findings from Indo-European languages, however, we did not observe unique surprisal effects at the lowest, phonemic level. Furthermore, the surprisal of lexical tone in Mandarin modulated brain activity only when integrated with its phonological components.

These findings suggest that predictive processing during Mandarin speech comprehension operates concurrently across multiple (though not necessarily all) levels of linguistic granularity, with its implementation shaped by language-specific structural properties.

Language comprehension involves segmenting a continuous acoustic stream into multiple linguistic units, from phonemes to words, and generating predictions at these levels. However, direct neural evidence remains limited regarding how segmentation and prediction operate simultaneously across levels of linguistic granularity, particularly outside Indo-European languages.

Recent findings suggest that using temporal response function analysis of magnetoencephalography data recorded during naturalistic Mandarin listening, we show that predictive processing occurs across multiple levels of linguistic granularity. Specifically, we find evidence for prediction-related neural responses at sub-syllabic, character, and word levels, but not a reliable unique effect at the phonemic level.

These results indicate that predictive processing also operates during Mandarin speech comprehension, and its neural implementation is shaped by language-specific structural properties.

The one number that changes everything.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Feeling frustrated on a Monday morning is not a reason to quit. But persistent patterns that affect your health, relationships, and long-term career growth are legitimate signals worth examining. The challenge is separating temporary frustration from genuine misalignment.

Recent findings suggest that the FI community approaches this differently from mainstream career advice. Instead of asking "Am I happy at work?" — which fluctuates daily — we ask: "Is this role aligned with my long-term financial and personal goals?" That reframe turns an emotional decision into a strategic one.

Before you submit your resignation, your finances need to be ready regardless of how miserable you are. Quitting without financial preparation trades one source of stress for another.

The FI community has a massive advantage here. If you have been building toward financial independence — even if you are not there yet — your savings provide a runway that most people do not have. A $200,000 investment portfolio at a 4% safe withdrawal rate provides $8,000 per year in sustainable income, which dramatically reduces the pressure of a job search.

The worst time to make a career decision is when you are emotionally overwhelmed. A terrible meeting, a passed-over promotion, or a toxic interaction with a coworker can make quitting feel urgent when the situation may actually be temporary or fixable.

Use the 30-day test: if you have wanted to quit for fewer than 30 consecutive days, it is likely a temporary frustration. If the feeling has persisted — or intensified — for 30+ days, it is a pattern worth taking seriously.

Sources indicate that how you leave a job matters as much as why you leave. Your professional reputation follows you for your entire career, and the people you work with today may be the hiring managers, clients, or references of tomorrow.

Recent findings suggest that two weeks notice: This is the minimum professional standard in the United States. For senior roles, three to four weeks is more appropriate. Check your employment contract — some roles require 30, 60, or 90 days notice.

According to recent reports, the resignation conversation: Schedule a private meeting with your direct manager. Keep it brief and positive. Say: "I have decided to move on to a upcoming opportunity. I want to thank you for [specific positive thing], and I am committed to making the transition as smooth as possible. My last day would be [date].".

Recent findings suggest that the transition strategy: Document your ongoing projects, key contacts, passwords, and processes. Offer to train your replacement. Complete as much outstanding work as possible. A strong exit creates goodwill that pays dividends for years.

What not to do: Do not badmouth the tech giant, your boss, or your coworkers — not in the resignation meeting, not in your exit interview, not on social media. Even if your grievances are legitimate, airing them publicly hurts your reputation more than theirs.
