Scientists find hidden driver of aging and a simple amino acid that fights memory loss in mice

📅 12 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1973 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • What if some of the changes we associate with aging begin with the loss of a single protein deep inside the brain?
  • The findings, originally published in March 2023 in PLOS Biology, came from researchers led by Lige Leng of Xiamen University in China.
  • Sources indicate that research published since then has added evidence that the brain plays an important role in regulating aging.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What if some of the changes we associate with aging begin with the loss of a single protein deep inside the brain? Scientists investigating that possibility found that restoring a protein called Menin in older mice improved memory, balance, bone mass, and skin thickness in just 30 days. Even more surprisingly, supplementing the animals with a naturally occurring amino acid improved their learning and memory in only three weeks.

The findings, originally published in March 2023 in PLOS Biology, came from researchers led by Lige Leng of Xiamen University in China. Their experiments identified a previously overlooked connection between inflammation, brain chemistry, and aging throughout the body. Although the results were obtained in mice, they raised an intriguing possibility: Some effects of aging may be influenced by biological processes in the brain that scientists could eventually learn to modify.

Sources indicate that research published since then has added evidence that the brain plays an important role in regulating aging. It has also revealed why the seemingly simple supplement findings deserve careful interpretation.

How a Hidden Brain Protein May Influence Aging.

At the center of the discovery is the hypothalamus, a small but powerful region near the base of the brain. It helps regulate essential functions such as body temperature, hunger, metabolism, sleep, and hormone production. Because these systems affect nearly every organ, changes in the hypothalamus can have consequences throughout the body.

It has been revealed that scientists have increasingly recognized the hypothalamus as an crucial player in aging. One possible reason involves neuroinflammation, the brain's inflammatory response. Although inflammation helps protect against infections and injuries, persistent inflammation can interfere with normal cellular function and contribute to age-related deterioration.

Earlier work by Leng and colleagues had identified Menin as a protein that helps restrain inflammation in the hypothalamus. Menin also participates in regulating gene activity, allowing it to influence multiple biological pathways.

The researchers wanted to understand what happens when this protective protein begins to disappear with age.

Industry observers note that they discovered that Menin levels gradually declined in certain hypothalamic neurons as mice grew older. Interestingly, the same decrease was not observed in astrocytes or microglia, two other important types of brain cells involved in supporting neurons and managing immune responses.

To investigate whether this decline actually contributed to aging, the team developed genetically modified mice in which Menin could be selectively disabled.

Recent findings suggest that the results were striking. Mice with reduced Menin activity developed greater inflammation in the hypothalamus, thinner skin, reduced bone mass, and worsening cognitive performance. Their lifespans were also modestly shortened.

Rather than simply accompanying aging, the loss of Menin appeared capable of helping drive several of its characteristic changes.

Restoring Menin Reversed Several Signs of Aging in 30 Days.

The researchers then asked an even more interesting question: If declining Menin contributes to aging, could restoring the protein reverse some of the damage?

According to recent reports, to find out, they used a gene delivery technique to increase Menin production in a specific part of the hypothalamus in older (20-month-old) mice. This region, called the ventromedial hypothalamus, helps coordinate metabolism, energy balance, and other bodily functions.

Just 30 days after treatment, the animals indicated measurable improvements.

Their skin became thicker, bone mass increased, and performance improved on tests measuring learning, memory, and balance. Researchers also observed reductions in inflammation and improvements in certain metabolic changes associated with aging.

In a separate survival analysis, mice receiving the Menin treatment also lived longer than untreated controls.

These findings suggested that some biological changes associated with old age could be at least partially reversed by restoring Menin activity in a specific group of brain cells.

But the researchers also uncovered an important clue about how Menin produced these effects.

A Simple Amino Acid Offers a Surprising Clue.

When Menin levels declined, the researchers noticed that concentrations of D-serine, an amino acid involved in brain signaling, also fell.

Sources indicate that amino acids are best known as the building blocks of proteins, but some perform other vital functions. D-serine helps regulate NMDA receptors, specialized proteins on nerve cells that are essential for communication between neurons, learning, and the formation of memories.

D-serine is closely related to L-serine, an amino acid commonly found in foods such as soybeans, eggs, fish, and nuts. The two forms have different biological roles. Although D-serine is also available as a dietary supplement, consuming ordinary serine-rich foods is not equivalent to taking the form used in the experiments.

Sources indicate that further investigation revealed that Menin helps control the production of PHGDH, an enzyme involved in the biochemical pathway that generates serine (which was in turn regulated by Menin). When Menin activity decreased, this pathway became less active, reducing the amount of D-serine available to the brain.

Restoring Menin increased D-serine levels in the hippocampus, a region especially key for learning and memory.

This connection suggested that the cognitive effects of declining Menin might be partly explained by disruptions in D-serine signaling.

To test the idea directly, the scientists gave older mice D-serine in their drinking water for three weeks.

The supplementation improved their performance on learning and memory tests, even without directly restoring Menin.

According to recent reports, however, there was an key distinction. While increasing Menin improved both cognitive function and physical signs of aging, D-serine supplementation primarily improved cognition. It did not restore the age-related losses in bone mass and skin thickness.

That difference suggests Menin influences aging through several biological mechanisms, with D-serine accounting for only part of its effects.

Later Research Strengthens the Link Between the Brain and Aging.

Since the original 2023 discovery, additional studies have provided evidence that the hypothalamus helps coordinate aging across the body.

In a 2024 study published in Cell Metabolism, researchers at Washington University School of Medicine identified a different group of hypothalamic neurons that communicates with fat tissue. By maintaining or stimulating this communication pathway, they increased physical activity, improved age-related metabolic function, and extended lifespan in mice.

That work involved a different protein and neural circuit from Menin, but supported the broader idea that signals originating in the hypothalamus can influence how the rest of the body ages.

Another 2024 study in the Journal of Physiology and Biochemistry provided additional insight into Menin itself. Researchers found that increasing Menin helped protect cultured hippocampal cells against inflammation and a form of programmed cell death triggered by exposure to the stress hormone corticosterone. Although these laboratory experiments did not establish an anti-aging effect, they supported the idea that Menin has important protective functions in brain cells.

An even larger picture emerged in January 2025, when scientists published a detailed analysis of approximately 1.2 million mouse brain cells in Nature.

The researchers discovered that some of the brain cells most sensitive to aging were concentrated around the third ventricle, a fluid-filled cavity in the hypothalamus. Many aging cells showed reduced activity in genes involved in normal neuronal function and increased activity in genes associated with inflammation and immune responses.

These findings highlighted the hypothalamus as a potential center of vulnerability during brain aging, although they did not directly test the Menin pathway.

Newly introduced Findings in 2026 Reveal More Aging Pathways.

Research published in 2026 has further strengthened the connection between hypothalamic activity and longevity.

In a study published in Cell, scientists found that strengthening daily biological rhythms in a specific hypothalamic region improved several aging-related measurements and extended lifespan in male mice. The intervention also reduced estimates of biological age based on DNA methylation, chemical modifications to DNA that change with age.

According to recent reports, another 2026 study in Cell Metabolism identified a protein called Mimecan that helps skeletal muscles communicate with the hypothalamus and brown fat, a specialized tissue involved in generating body heat. Restoring circulating Mimecan levels in older mice improved this communication and extended lifespan.

Together, these discoveries suggest that aging involves complex communication between the brain and the rest of the body. Rather than depending on one master switch, multiple neural circuits, hormones, and metabolic signals appear to help determine how age-related changes unfold.

Could D-Serine Supplements Protect the Human Brain?

The possibility of improving memory with a relatively simple amino acid is especially appealing. However, evidence that D-serine can reverse age-related cognitive decline in humans remains limited.

A small randomized clinical trial published in 2016 tested D-serine in 50 healthy older adults. Participants performed better on one assessment of spatial learning and problem-solving after receiving the amino acid, but researchers did not find significant improvements across the other cognitive tests or mood measurements.

More importantly, later research suggests that the effects of D-serine depend on the biological circumstances.

In an April 2025 study published in Cellular and Molecular Life Sciences, scientists investigated D-serine in mice genetically engineered to develop features of Alzheimer's disease.

Unlike the Menin experiments, which associated reduced D-serine with age-related memory impairment, this study found that an early increase in D-serine accompanied disruptions in brain signaling. Removing the enzyme responsible for producing D-serine prevented or reduced several later cognitive impairments in those mice.

According to recent reports, these findings do not invalidate the earlier results. Instead, they suggest that D-serine signaling is more complicated than simply having too little or too much. Its effects may depend on the condition being studied, the timing of treatment, and how the brain's signaling systems are functioning.

Recent findings suggest that there are also unanswered questions about the long-term safety of D-serine supplementation. High doses have raised kidney safety concerns in animal experiments, and research has not established whether prolonged supplementation is a safe or effective way to prevent age-related memory loss in otherwise healthy people.

For now, D-serine should be considered an experimental approach rather than a proven treatment for brain aging.

Can Scientists Eventually Slow Aging by Targeting the Brain?

Despite the encouraging mouse experiments, researchers still need to answer several fundamental questions.

In a recent development, why does Menin decline in the hypothalamus as animals age? How many of its effects could be reversed by treatment, and how long would those improvements last? Could restoring Menin influence other biological systems in unexpected ways?

It is also unclear whether treatments targeting Menin or D-serine could reproduce similar results in humans.

Nevertheless, the original researchers believe the pathway deserves further investigation.

Industry observers note that "We speculate that the decline of Menin expression in the hypothalamus with age may be one of the driving factors of aging, and Menin may be the key protein connecting the genetic, inflammatory, and metabolic factors of aging. D-serine is a potentially promising therapeutic for cognitive decline," mentioned Leng.

It has been revealed that leng adds, "Ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH) Menin signaling diminished in aged mice, which contributes to systemic aging phenotypes and cognitive deficits. The effects of Menin on aging are mediated by neuroinflammatory changes and metabolic pathway signaling, accompanied by serine deficiency in VMH, while restoration of Menin in VMH reversed aging-related phenotypes.".

Recent findings suggest that the growing body of evidence points toward a potentially notable shift in how scientists understand aging. Instead of viewing it only as the gradual deterioration of individual organs, researchers are investigating how specific brain pathways may actively shape the process.

It has been revealed that the possibility that restoring those pathways could improve memory, physical function, or longevity remains experimental. But the Menin discovery, together with subsequent findings, offers a compelling reason to explore whether some of the biological changes associated with aging are more reversible than previously thought.

Five Things Students Taught Us About Connecting Across Differences

📅 28 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2606 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, when I’m producing a documentary, one of my favorite parts of the process is the moment when a bit of our footage sticks to me.
  • Sources indicate that often it’s a funny line—a perfect, punchy distillation of the truth that gets adopted as an inside joke among the team of producers and editors.
  • For the better part of the past year, I’ve been working as an executive producer on a series of short documentaries for the Greater Good Science Center called Connecting on Campus: Stories of Courage, Curiosity, and Empathy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, when I’m producing a documentary, one of my favorite parts of the process is the moment when a bit of our footage sticks to me. Permanently. I never know when it will happen, but it always does. The sticky bit could be a snippet of dialogue or a quote from an interview. After watching the footage over and over again, the bit becomes part of me.

Sources indicate that often it’s a funny line—a perfect, punchy distillation of the truth that gets adopted as an inside joke among the team of producers and editors. We repeat it like a collective spell that buoys us when we’re sinking under the weight of the project’s heavy subject matter. Sometimes the thing that sticks is not funny at all. Sometimes it’s a splinter, a cutting insight that I would have rather avoided. Or it’s a solidly true, heartfelt moment that sits like a smooth stone in my pocket. The touchstone grounds and guides me on the long journey of making a film.

For the better part of the past year, I’ve been working as an executive producer on a series of short documentaries for the Greater Good Science Center called Connecting on Campus: Stories of Courage, Curiosity, and Empathy. The series features students at four universities across the country who are attempting to connect in some meaningful way with people who have different life experiences, political beliefs, or visions for the future.

In a recent development, at Iliff School of Theology, master’s and Ph.D. students imagine a version of the United States that embodies their values, and then they share those visions with one another. As they listen to one another’s values, they discover where they align, where they diverge, and where empathy can keep them in relationship with each other even when they disagree.

In a two-part story set at Bowie State University and the University of Maryland, students from both campuses gather at an event hosted by the schools’ Social Justice Alliance, a first-of-its-kind collaboration between an HBCU (historically Black college or university) and a PWI (predominantly white institution).

Industry observers note that at Dickinson College, a deep friendship between the presidents of the Dickinson College Republicans and the Dickinson College Democrats creates the conditions for an unexpectedly collaborative relationship between the two clubs. Members of both clubs gather regularly and listen to each other’s thoughts about complex and often contentious political issues.

Back when we were in the middle of editing these episodes with our collaborators at Anaconda Street Productions, I spent an afternoon reviewing footage from one of the shoots, and then I took my dog for a walk. On the walk, I found myself repeating a line from an interview. It stuck! It’s been one of those smooth stones in my pocket ever since.

Recent findings suggest that of course, I’m not the only one who was changed by the experience of working on this series. To celebrate the release of Connecting on Campus, I invite you behind the scenes to meet my collaborators as we share some of the many things we learned as we helped tell these stories.

It’s a pretty straightforward message, yet I hear it over and over in my head in the voice of Mrs. Dawn Collins. Your voice matters and everyone has a part to play. Mrs. Collins says these words during an interview in the first of our two episodes about Bowie State University (BSU) and the University of Maryland (UMD). Mrs. Collins and her husband, Mr. Richard Collins Jr., founded the BSU–UMD Social Justice Alliance after their son, Lt. Richard Collins III, a BSU student, was murdered on the UMD campus by a student in 2017. The Alliance brings together faculty, staff, and students to join the Collins’s commitment to “eradicating the ideology of intolerance, while confronting individuals and combatting systems that normalize indifference, justify injustice, perpetuate hate, and inflict violence.”.

Mrs. Collins’s words have stuck with me, in part, because they insist on every person’s dignity, power, and responsibility. Our voices matter, and we all have a role to play in eradicating the ideology of intolerance and in combatting systems that perpetuate hate and inflict violence. That’s a strong call to action.

In a recent development, mrs. Collins’s words have also stuck with me because they clearly articulate the heart of this documentary series. The students featured in this series offer us examples of what happens when people step into their power and accept the responsibility to understand themselves, understand each other (differences and all), and work together to build something fresh. That new thing could be a collaboration between clubs on campus or a vision for our future as a nation. Either way, these students know their voices matter and they have what it takes to practice doing this work together.

It was so helpful to have Mrs. Collins’s voice in my head, keeping me anchored in this truth as I worked. — Kelly Rafferty.

When we first imagined Connecting on Campus, we wanted to find places where students were actually practicing the skills and qualities that make connection across differences possible, and to make those moments visible.

As I spent time with these students and their stories, and as we shaped the episodes in the edit, I found myself thinking more and more about choice. Across the series, you see students staying curious when they could shut down, listening to understand someone else’s experience, sharing their own perspective while making space for someone else’s, or finding the courage to remain in a difficult conversation.

In a recent development, in our Dickinson College episode, that choice shows up in a moment that could have easily passed. Ryan Thies recounts meeting Matthew Craig at a Halloween party during his freshman year. Matthew was dressed as Donald Trump. Ryan could have seen that costume, made an assumption about who Matthew was, and walked away. Instead, he leaned in and got to know him. An unlikely connection became a friendship, and eventually the two chose to become roommates. Ryan’s choice changed what became possible between them. That choice reflects the kind of empathy we talk about in our Bridging Differences work: the deliberate, and often difficult, choice to engage with someone else’s experience even when it feels unfamiliar or challenges our own worldview.

Recent findings suggest that the choices look different in our Bowie State University and University of Maryland episodes—and the stakes are obviously very different, too. Here, the students and the Collins family are stepping into a history that is devastating: the murder of Lt. Richard Collins III on the University of Maryland campus and the work that emerged from it to confront hatred and bring students from the two campuses together.

Here, courage looks like choosing to show up and engage when discomfort, conflict, and fear might make it easier—and completely understandable—to withdraw. It’s the decision to say: This matters. I’ll attend. I’ll represent. I’ll listen. I’ll do my part.

Practices like “Listen with Empathy,” “Understand Their Values,” “Expand Your Views and Circles,” or “Perspective Giving and Getting” from our Bridging Differences in Higher Education Playbook can be learned.

Industry observers note that but the choice to engage is one each of us has to make. My hope is that people watch these stories asking themselves, “What did that person do that made greater understanding possible, and where might I try that myself?”  — Juliana Tafur.

I came away thinking that “bridging” is sometimes misunderstood as compromise. Across all four videos, something more interesting emerges: You can build a relationship across a difference without necessarily resolving the difference itself.

At Iliff School of Theology, students imagine very different versions of America without being asked to arrive at one shared vision. At Dickinson, Republicans and Democrats engage seriously with each other without abandoning their political beliefs. And at Bowie State University and the University of Maryland, students move beyond assumptions, allow themselves to be vulnerable, ask difficult questions, and really listen to people whose backgrounds and experiences differ from their own. The circumstances are very different, but the lesson is consistent: Bridging isn’t about erasing what separates us. It’s about developing the curiosity, trust, and courage to stay connected across those differences.

The series asks a harder and more useful question than “How do we get everyone to agree?” It asks how we live, learn, and build community with people who may never see the world exactly as we do. The answers aren’t presented as a formula. You get to watch people experiment with listening, vulnerability, curiosity, disagreement, and repair, then decide for yourself what actually works. — Omar Lugones.

Sources indicate that in my own experiences in smaller, more intimate classroom settings, I often observe an echo-chamber effect when opinions are shared, especially when the class is discussing a controversial topic. I have noticed a general apprehension about “going first” or initiating the conversation. Speaking for myself, I am often afraid of offering the “wrong” opinion, meaning a perspective that could be interpreted as supporting a politically or socially unacceptable position and cause my peers to view me as an outsider. I do not necessarily think my peers are experiencing the exact same thought process, but I sense that they are also self-conscious about expressing a conflicting opinion. As a result, people may default to agreeing with whoever offers an opinion first.

I thought it was remarkable that at Iliff School of Theology, Lindsay Ambler and Stephanie Nelson initially disagree with one another, and that moment opens space for others to enter the conversation and offer their own perspectives. By disagreeing respectfully, they demonstrate how disagreement can produce a deeper understanding of an problem than a conversation built only around agreement.

Lindsay takes a strong position on the effects of religion based on her past experiences with Christian institutions. By sharing an extremely vulnerable personal story, she creates the conditions for others to share their experiences and, in turn, promotes a greater sense of empathy within the conversation.

When Stephanie offers her own perspective on whether society can reach a state of perfection and equality, her response conflicts with Lindsay’s position. This point of contention could seemingly disrupt the vulnerable environment Lindsay has created, yet it does not. Instead, Lindsay responds to the challenge by deepening her explanation. In doing so, she creates new points of entry for others to join the conversation and contribute their own experiences.

At the end of the discussion, Stephanie expresses gratitude to those who shared their perspectives and revealed gaps in her own thinking. The conversation demonstrates how respectful disagreement can foster empathy, growth, and greater participation from every member of a group. — Tyler C. Tang.

Sources indicate that working on this series, I noticed the relationship between character and discomfort. Courage, empathy, humility, and curiosity all sound admirable in the abstract, but you really discover whether you possess them when another person challenges you. Character in these films often reveals itself in what someone does immediately after hearing something they don’t agree with.

Industry observers note that for example, I identified with Josh Perez, a Ph.D. student and teaching assistant at Iliff School of Theology, in particular. I appreciate the way he draws on his own experiences as a second-generation Mexican American while recognizing that other people carry struggles he may never experience himself. His vision isn’t simply about creating a world that works better for people like him. It’s about making room for others to find liberation from their own struggles, as well. That ability to be grounded in your own experience while still making space for the experiences of others is at the heart of bridging differences. — Antonio Carrasco III.

Sources indicate that if you’re exhausted by watching people argue about politics, identity, and social issues, watch people actually talk to each other instead. The series doesn’t suggest that differences disappear when people sit down together. It highlights that disagreement can be productive when people approach each other with curiosity and humility.

It has been revealed that iliff School of Theology student Lindsay Ambler’s story affected me in a way I didn’t expect. It was hard to hear how painful some of her experiences within religious spaces had been. Learning how she was rejected after people discovered she was gay gave me a much deeper understanding of what she carried into the classroom. It reminded me how little we may know about someone until we give them the space to share their story.

Sources indicate that logan Midler from the University of Maryland stands out to me, too. I appreciate how honest she is about not having much interaction with people from different backgrounds and how easy it can be to start those conversations. Her desire to listen, learn, and become a better ally feels like a simple yet powerful example of bridging differences. — Ryan Carrasco.

I hope there’s a moment in Connecting on Campus that sticks with you, too. Maybe that memorable line, that bit of dialogue, or that mindful pause will become a touchstone for your own experiments in bridging differences.

As another academic year begins, may the stories in this series also serve as an example of what students are capable of doing when they’re given the space and support to practice connecting with one another. Campuses across the country are facing real challenges—everything from threats of censorship to rising costs and cuts to funding—and these opportunities to practice bridging differences must not be sacrificed along the way. They’re too important to our individual and collective well-being.

Watch Connecting on Campus: Stories of Courage, Curiosity, and Empathy.

#173442. Scientists uncover a hidden map of the brain with 539 distinct regions

Scientists uncover a hidden map of the brain with 539 distinct regions

📅 13 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (939 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists have spent decades studying the brain's cells, connections, genes, and proteins.
  • Although lipids are fundamental to brain function, scientists have struggled to map where different types are located.
  • "So scientists have had only a blurry picture of how lipids differ from one part of the brain to another," says Giovanni D'Angelo, professor at The Kristian Gerhard Jebsen Foundation Chair in Nutrition and Metabolism at EPFL.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists have spent decades studying the brain's cells, connections, genes, and proteins. Yet another essential part of brain biology has received far less attention: lipids. These fatty molecules make up the membranes surrounding neurons, contribute to the myelin insulation that protects nerve fibers, and play crucial roles in communication between brain cells.

Although lipids are fundamental to brain function, scientists have struggled to map where different types are located. Conventional imaging techniques cannot easily distinguish individual lipid molecules, leaving a major gap in our understanding of the brain's chemical organization.

"So scientists have had only a blurry picture of how lipids differ from one part of the brain to another," says Giovanni D'Angelo, professor at The Kristian Gerhard Jebsen Foundation Chair in Nutrition and Metabolism at EPFL. "That gap matters, because changes in brain lipids are increasingly linked to conditions from depression to Alzheimer's disease.".

Industry observers note that researchers at EPFL have now taken a major step toward filling that gap. A team led by D'Angelo, Luca Fusar Bassini, and Gioele La Manno has created a detailed map showing how lipids are distributed throughout the mouse brain.

Their Lipid Brain Atlas reveals that these molecules are arranged in highly organized patterns. Some match familiar anatomical structures, while others expose chemical boundaries that previous approaches had overlooked. The patterns are so distinctive that researchers could identify where a brain tissue sample originated simply by examining its lipid composition.

The findings were published in Nature.

Scientists Identify 539 Distinct Chemical Zones in the Brain.

To construct the atlas, researchers used mass spectrometry imaging, a technique that allows them to identify lipid molecules across thin sections of brain tissue. A laser scans each slice one location at a time, producing detailed information about which lipids are present and where they are found.

Recent findings suggest that the team examined 172 different lipids in 109 brain slices collected from 11 mice. This generated approximately 7 million measurements, which scientists combined into a comprehensive 3D reconstruction using machine learning tools developed specifically for the project.

The resulting atlas revealed 539 chemically distinct territories, which the researchers named "lipizones." Each has a characteristic combination of lipids, creating a recognizable chemical signature.

Many of these regions correspond to established brain structures and cell types. Others reveal unexpected relationships between groups of nerve cell bodies and distant regions connected by their fibers. Such connections have often been difficult to detect using maps based on gene activity.

"In effect, lipids work like postal codes, giving distant but related parts of the brain the same chemical address," says D'Angelo.

Hidden Chemical Patterns Challenge Previous Brain Maps.

The new atlas also uncovered surprising differences within parts of the brain that scientists previously considered relatively uniform.

One striking example is white matter, the tissue containing nerve fibers that connect different brain regions. Rather than having a largely consistent chemical composition, white matter contains numerous distinct lipid zones.

"This reveals that the cells which make myelin are far more varied in their chemistry than their genes alone would suggest," indicates Luca Fusar Bassini.

The researchers also detected previously unrecognized chemical boundaries in the choroid plexus, the structure responsible for producing cerebrospinal fluid, as well as in the tissues lining the brain's internal cavities.

Together, these findings show that lipid mapping can reveal important features of brain organization that are not apparent from anatomy or genetic information alone.

Pregnancy Triggers Widespread Changes in Brain Lipids.

Beyond identifying the brain's chemical structure, the atlas offered new insight into how that structure changes during pregnancy.

In a recent development, when researchers examined pregnant mice, they found substantial shifts in lipid composition across numerous brain regions. Overall, these changes were more pronounced than the typical lipid differences observed between male and female mice.

The cortex, which forms the brain's outer layer, showed particularly extensive changes. Meanwhile, levels of galactosyl ceramide, an key component of myelin, increased sharply throughout much of the brain's white matter.

These findings suggest that pregnancy involves significant changes in the brain's chemical makeup, potentially helping its neural connections adapt to the body's changing demands.

"Together, these shifts suggest the brain retunes its own wiring to meet the demands of pregnancy," says Gioele La Manno. "The Atlas reveals that the brain constantly adjusts its lipids to meet the body's changing needs.".

A New Tool for Understanding Brain Aging and Disease.

The Lipid Brain Atlas is freely available online, allowing scientists worldwide to explore this previously difficult-to-study aspect of brain biology.

By combining lipid information with existing genetic and cellular maps, researchers can gain a more complete understanding of how the brain is organized and how its chemistry changes over time.

The atlas also establishes a detailed reference for healthy mouse brain tissue. Scientists can use it to investigate how disruptions in lipid distribution might contribute to brain development, aging, and disorders such as Alzheimer's disease and depression.

Although the specific mouse brain map cannot be directly applied to humans, the approach used to create it could help researchers uncover comparable patterns in the human brain.

"What transfers to humans isn't the map, it's the method, and the fact that we now know that a healthy brain has a very organized lipid map at all," says Luca Fusar Bassini.

Russian strikes damage historic buildings in Kyiv and Odesa, including World Heritage sites

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Multiple heritage sites in Ukraine were damaged by Russian strikes on 19 and 20 November, including the Unesco-listed St Michael’s Golden-Domed Cathedral and Monastery complex and St Volodymyr’s Cathedral in Kyiv, known for its frescoes, as well as 12 cultural heritage sites in Odesa, the strategic port city on the Black Sea, which was hit a day earlier. The entire historic centre of Odesa was added to Unesco’s list of endangered World Heritage sites in 2023.

At least nine people were killed in Kyiv and other regions of Ukraine during the hours-long attack on 20 November.

“Today, Russian drones damaged one of the most famous monuments of our country, the Volodymyr Cathedral,” Tetyana Berezhna, Ukraine’s deputy prime minister for humanitarian policy and minister of culture, wrote in a Facebook post on 19 November after the cathedral in Kyiv was hit, breaking windows and frames and causing “some damage to the paintings and structural elements”.

According to recent reports, the neo-Byzantine St Volodymyr Cathedral, built in the 19th century, is under the jurisdiction of the Orthodox Church of Ukraine (OCU), which broke with the Moscow Patriarchate and was granted autocephaly by Constantinople in 2018. Three of Russia’s most famous artists of the 19th century and early 20th century—Viktor Vasnetsov, Mikhail Vrubel and Mikhail Nesterov—created religious art for St Volodymyr’s, as did the Ukrainian artist Mykola Pymomenko, a teacher of Kazimir Malevich.

Industry observers note that the Austrian embassy, located next-door to St Volodymyr's Cathedral, was also damaged. Kyiv's municipal cultural heritage department published an inventory of damage from the attack, which also includes the embassy of the Netherlands.

A Russian drone was shot down over St Michael’s, which is the headquarters of the OCU, on 19 November.

In a recent development, berezhna’s post cites the cumulative damage from Russia’s accelerating attacks: “Since the beginning of this year, the number of monuments damaged by Russia has increased by more than a third, and by the end of October it was almost 2,200. Almost 2,700 cultural institutions were also affected.”.

The minister was in Lutsk, a historic city in northwestern Ukraine, this week to plan for a conference marking the 600th anniversary in 2029 of the Congress of Lutsk, which brought together the regional monarchies of the time. A Russian strike on Lutsk in October damaged Ukraine’s largest painting, Cosmogony, a 2,000 sq. m work by the contemporary artist Petro Antyp.

In a recent development, unesco has condemned the latest attacks, especially on Odesa, “which hit the centre of the city, within the boundaries of the World Heritage property ‘The Historic Centre of Odesa’” and “reportedly caused damage to several heritage buildings, including the Kalio Palace, a monument of national importance,” according to a statement released by the organisation. The Kalio Palace, built in 1834, is attributed to the Swiss Italian architect Giorgio Torricelli.

Sources indicate that the strikes came amid escalating tensions and a diplomatic chasm that appears to be widening. The Russian President Vladimir Putin stated this week that the Kremlin would not negotiate any partial ceasefire or deal with Ukraine after it struck and incapacitated the Kerch Bridge linking mainland Russia to Crimea, a symbol of Russia’s annexation of the Black Sea peninsula in 2014, on 16 and 17 November. At the same time, US President Donald Trump claimed that peace, largely on Russia’s terms, is within reach and reportedly urged European leaders to stop funding weapons for Ukraine. Trump, Putin and the Chinese President Xi Jinping signed a “peace declaration” on 20 November at a trilateral summit hosted by Xi in Shenzhen, China.

A petition to “safeguard Ukraine’s cultural heritage and artistic integrity” was launched last month by the curator Konstantin Akinsha and Bjorn Geldof, the artistic director at Kyiv’s PinchukArtCentre. It calls “for immediate sanctions and the suspension of Russian state participation in international cultural events”. Rapporteur, a Brussels-based policy publication, reported this week that ten European countries are seeking to keep Russia out of the 2027 Architecture Biennale. Russia’s participation in the 2026 Venice Biennale set off a series of protests.

#173439. The secret to handling stress better may start at breakfast

📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

The secret to handling stress better may start at breakfast

📅 13 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (685 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that feeling overwhelmed by stress or struggling to adjust when things go wrong?
  • Upcoming research from Binghamton University suggests that these healthy routines are connected to a mental skill called psychological flexibility, which helps people adapt to challenges and recover from stressful experiences.
  • Sources indicate that psychological flexibility refers to the ability to adjust your thoughts, emotions, and actions as circumstances change.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that feeling overwhelmed by stress or struggling to adjust when things go wrong? Everyday habits such as eating a nutritious breakfast, getting regular exercise, and sleeping enough may play an important role in how well your mind handles difficult situations.

Upcoming research from Binghamton University suggests that these healthy routines are connected to a mental skill called psychological flexibility, which helps people adapt to challenges and recover from stressful experiences.

Sources indicate that psychological flexibility refers to the ability to adjust your thoughts, emotions, and actions as circumstances change. Rather than becoming trapped in negative thinking or overwhelmed by frustration, people with greater psychological flexibility can recognize their emotions, consider their options, and respond in a more productive way.

Industry observers note that "You might know someone who stays cool under pressure," said Lina Begdache, an associate professor of health and wellness studies at Binghamton University and lead author of the research. "The kind of person who misses a flight and, instead of panicking, calmly adapts to the situation. This person may still feel stressed, but they're better able to manage it through psychological flexibility.".

"People may say that these are resilient people, but they also have what's called psychological flexibility. They're able to change the way they think about the situation and then use brain resources to handle the stress.".

How Breakfast, Sleep, and Exercise Relate to Mental Resilience.

It has been revealed that to explore the relationship between lifestyle choices and emotional resilience, Begdache worked with Jason Cherry, a former Binghamton assistant professor of physical therapy, and former student Alexander J. Talkachov.

The researchers collected anonymous survey responses from approximately 400 college students, gathering information about their diets, sleep patterns, exercise habits, and other lifestyle factors.

Sources indicate that their findings revealed an important connection between healthy routines and the ability to cope with stress. Students who reported healthier habits, including regular physical activity and consistent breakfast consumption, also tended to demonstrate greater psychological flexibility and resilience.

The study identified several notable associations:.

The opposite pattern also emerged. Students who reported less healthy behaviors, including frequent fast food consumption and insufficient sleep, tended to show greater psychological rigidity, meaning they had more difficulty adjusting their thoughts and behaviors when circumstances changed.

Because the research relied on survey responses, the results demonstrate associations rather than proving that these habits directly improve psychological flexibility or resilience.

Why Psychological Flexibility Matters for Stress.

According to Begdache, psychological flexibility gives people the mental space to recognize what they are experiencing instead of becoming completely absorbed by their stress. This ability to reassess a situation can make it easier to understand difficult emotions and determine how to respond.

She explained that improvements in diet and lifestyle may help support this kind of mental adaptability.

Recent findings suggest that "When we're under stress, we feel like we fuse with the stress. We live the stress. But psychological flexibility is like stepping back and thinking, 'I feel this because of that. What can I do?' Identifying your emotions sometimes helps you find the solution for these emotions," said Begdache.

The findings also build on Begdache's previous research, which linked nutritious diets to greater resilience and poorer dietary habits to reduced resilience.

The latest study offers a possible explanation for that relationship. Rather than influencing resilience alone, diet and lifestyle may support psychological flexibility, which in turn helps people manage stress more effectively.

Sources indicate that "The new finding here is that diet and lifestyle don't just make you resilient by themselves. They help you build the psychological flexibility, which, in turn, makes you a resilient person.".

The study, "Dietary and lifestyle factors and resilience: the role of psychological flexibility as a mediator," was published in the Journal of American College Health.

Materials provided by Binghamton University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#173438. You Might Be Experiencing Rustout, Not Burnout, at Work

📅 28 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1683 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Berkeley ↗ Open Full Page

You Might Be Experiencing Rustout, Not Burnout, at Work

📅 28 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1683 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, some forms of distress at work are easy to recognize because they interrupt someone’s daily performance and the work of those around them: For example, a person on your team becomes visibly exhausted, they are irritable, or they’re frequently absent.
  • It’s common to talk about burnout at work and to recognize it in others and in ourselves.
  • Rustout, as we studied it, often involves being underutilized, intellectually stagnating, and feeling a deep-seated sense of unfulfillment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, some forms of distress at work are easy to recognize because they interrupt someone’s daily performance and the work of those around them: For example, a person on your team becomes visibly exhausted, they are irritable, or they’re frequently absent. But other forms of distress are harder to see precisely because the work continues uninterrupted.

It’s common to talk about burnout at work and to recognize it in others and in ourselves. But a upcoming paper of mine with David S. Smith examines a less visible and less understood form of disengagement at work: rustout.

Rustout, as we studied it, often involves being underutilized, intellectually stagnating, and feeling a deep-seated sense of unfulfillment. It can arise when people feel their work no longer offers enough meaning or challenge to keep them intellectually and creatively engaged. But because it’s different from burnout, the solutions are also different—both for individuals and for organizations.

I’ve presented this research at numerous conferences, and each time I have been approached by professionals who say, “That’s what I’ve been going through, but I never had a name for it until now.”.

These people, young and older, are committed to their work, they are hardworking, and they haven’t stopped caring. It is often the case that they care very much, and they meet expectations set before them. They are often the ones who are called upon because they are reliable and highly conscientious.

If you look around your workplace, you probably know many people who fit this bill. The problem is not a loss of effort on the part of the individual; it is a breakdown in the relationship between effort and meaningful work. From my study of this topic, rustout is really about the decline in professional vitality, when a person’s capacities are not used in ways that feel meaningful to them.

In our research, participants described experiences shaped by administrative overload, reduced autonomy, and a misalignment between their professional aspirations and assigned tasks. Many people highlighted feeling professionally stuck: “Sadly, the elements I love about the job . . . are often overshadowed by the other administrative aspects of the role,” “I feel like I’m feeding the machine,” and “I’m a square peg in a round hole.”.

They highlighted a sense that the work they were doing no longer drew sufficiently on their talents: “The better you are at it, the more of the administrative side of the job you get. It’s lacking opportunities to be creative.”.

Industry observers note that rustout can be quite psychologically disorienting. From the outside, a person may appear successful and competent. There is no question about their productivity; they meet set targets, but could do so “with [their] eyes closed.” However, they may feel increasingly detached from the work that once animated them. Their distress isn’t dramatic; it’s a slow process of psychological erosion.

Industry observers note that in many ways, rustout overlaps with burnout, but they are not the same. Burnout involves prolonged negative stress that isn’t adequately managed. It’s about too much—working too much, caring too much, too much pressure, and too little time to recuperate. In contrast, rustout is associated with too little positive stress or challenge over time, too little stimulation, and limited opportunities for individual growth.

Sources indicate that however, while burnout is part of organizations’ mental health literacy, rustout rarely gets a mention. And this is problematic—both for the individual and the organization. “I often feel I have produced nothing at the end of the week, and there is no sense of development,” one person noted.

Some will stay in their roles out of a sense of duty (and for other practical reasons like salary or seniority), but others will choose to leave. Another said, “I am functioning at my job, but I’m not thriving, and I am looking elsewhere.”.

According to recent reports, rustout often hides behind competence, and the reliable person is often given more of the same work. The person who does not complain is assumed to be coping and doing OK. The person who stabilizes others and is a good team player is rarely asked whether they themselves feel developed or challenged.

It has been revealed that one person remarked, “I have no experience of ever having a conversation with anyone around it. No line manager ever named it, it has never been mentioned in a communal setting or in a one-to-one setting. . . . No one has ever asked, ‘Do you feel fulfilled or do you feel you have opportunities to use your skills and talents in a meaningful way?’”.

In a recent development, it’s easy to see how doing overtime and being dependable can become a trap. Eventually, the employee becomes valued less for what they might become and more for what they can continue to absorb—they won’t “rock the boat” by opening the can of worms that is their dissatisfaction. “You put up, and shut up,” one person said.

Boost satisfaction, engagement, and collaboration with this three-course series.

In a recent development, meanwhile, many workplaces are organized to detect individual or team shortcomings (or failure) more readily than stagnation. If someone stops performing, the problem becomes visible. However, if someone continues to perform while becoming inwardly disengaged, the organization may see no problem at all. And if anyone notices their dissatisfaction, they may not openly discuss it, as another of my interviewees reported. “It suits everyone not to talk about it; when everyone is working and doing their jobs—then don’t disturb anything. Everything is cosy.”.

Participants experiencing rustout described barriers that limited their ability to use their strengths or pursue professional growth, which are particularly important for having a sense of meaning and fulfillment at work.

For many people, their working life gives them a sense of identity and purpose, but when work no longer offers that sense of meaning, their relationship with the job can become fractured or feel “off.” In some cases, they can’t put their finger on what is happening, and that might be why I often hear after presentations, “I never had a name for it.”.

It has been revealed that naming rustout won’t solve the issue, but it can help the person to understand why they feel underutilized or dissatisfied. Naming rustout can help people understand this isn’t a personal failure but an experience that is shaped by the design or conditions of work (much like burnout). It is also shaped by the culture of work, particularly when there is a resistance to change or a failure to see the value in helping people to flourish.

Sources indicate that from my discussions with participants and colleagues about rustout, it is clear that it isn’t a pre-retirement phenomenon. It seems to arise for those who are experienced, perhaps mid-career, and those who have been in their role for a long time.

One participant explained, “I have been doing [this role] for years. There must be better ways to organize things to ensure the expertise of experienced staff is used in more effective ways.” Others stated, “It’s the seven-, eight-, nine-year mark when there isn’t an opportunity to be stimulated,” and “It’s the seven-year itch, you’ve been doing something creative and then you reach a point where you are doing the same thing on repeat.”.

In such ways, we can’t dismiss rustout as a consequence of aging in the workplace. It can happen whenever people are pigeonholed into a system that no longer offers them meaningful development. Although some repetition and routine are an expected part of every job, there should also be a sense that your abilities and talents matter in your role. That there is a future and something exciting to work toward.

It has been revealed that the language of burnout has helped many people name distress that had previously been normalized or dismissed. It has also helped organizations take workplace well-being more seriously. But any dominant mental health vocabulary can become limiting when it starts to stand in for the whole field of experience. If burnout is the only category available for occupational distress, then recovery is often imagined in terms of rest and resilience.

They may be necessary, but they are not always sufficient. A person experiencing rustout may not simply need less work; they may need different work: work that restores their sense of intellectual engagement and curiosity. As Maya Angelou once said, “We aren’t designed to be static”—that could apply to all aspects of life, including the workplace.

Industry observers note that if you are experiencing rustout, it would be good to do an inventory of what is happening for you. Do you feel fulfilled in your role? Do you have opportunities to use your talents? Do you gain some sense of meaning from your role? Are there ways to seek renewal in your work? What might this look like, and can you have this conversation with your line manager or boss?

For organizations, the questions are also direct. Look around your team. Are you giving your most dependable employees opportunities for development? Do you continually lean on their “safe pair of hands” because it is easier than asking someone else to learn the ropes? Are you willing to put the conversation about professional dissatisfaction on the table? How can you help your team to flourish?

It has been revealed that that is the unsettling truth at the heart of the rustout. A person can be conscientious yet disengaged, reliable yet underused, competent but unfulfilled. They can be good at their job and still feel themselves receding from it. The silence around rustout allows it to thrive, which is why I often hear the same response after conference presentations: “I thought it was just me.” I think there is a particular loneliness in that sentence, the loneliness of continuing to do the work, while privately wondering why it no longer feels like yours.

Sources indicate that sabrina Fitzsimons, Ph.D., is a lecturer at Dublin City University, Ireland. Her research combines expertise in educators’ occupational well-being, mental health, and online environments.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Made Thought builds the Juana brand identity on acid lime and amber, a CBD skincare system where dense label type meets macro botanical light.

Juana is a CBD-powered skincare brand, and Made Thought frames it as half family tradition, half skincare innovation. Founder Yann Moujawaz comes from a line of surgeons and Syrian olive grove stewards, and his formulations aim to switch on the skin's own renewal with expert precision. The design answers a market full of noise and false claims with something that looks like proof: warm amber glass, clinical label density, and botanical photography shot like evidence. The palette does the arguing. Acid lime cuts against deep olive and burnt orange, and the amber packs glow against it all like samples held up to the light.

The wordmark is a compact grotesque JUANA in capitals, set small and quiet on every pack, letting the label copy do the talking. On the lime tubes, ingredient lists run down the barrel in tight bilingual columns, English beside French, with the CBD strength called out large: 100mg on the cleanser, 300mg on the face cream, plus vitamin E, jojoba oil, and hyaluronic acid in the same breath.

At poster scale the same type goes loud. Nurture Facial Cleanser, 100mg CBD fills the frame in acid lime, underlined, with the pack leaning into the shot. The web panel pairs a flat lime block reading Full Spectrum Cannabinoids with a hand dipping into a jar, and a line-drawn diagram of the whole range sits on olive like a spec sheet. The system holds together because the grid never changes, only the scale does.

The materials carry the science half of the story. Amber glass keeps the formulas away from the light, frosted lime plastic softens the tubes, and matte black caps close every silhouette. White outer cartons stack in a stepped row with a single lime band along the top edge, the only colour the box allows itself. Macro shots push closer still: a pipette suspended in fortifying face oil, bubbles rising through amber, and a leaf photographed so tight its veins turn into a map of yellow, green, and blue.

Founder Yann Moujawaz calls the partnership magic, saying passion was generously poured into it, and the photography backs him up. Nothing here is styled to look expensive for its own sake. The glow comes from the product itself, amber oil against orange light, and the identity lets it show.

#173436. Yale scientists discover how stress changes the brain to make memories stronger

📅 16 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1176 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Yale scientists discover how stress changes the brain to make memories stronger

📅 16 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1176 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that stress does more than influence how we feel.
  • Researchers at Yale University have now uncovered important clues.
  • "We all experience stress, and my lab is interested in understanding how stress can be helpful," stated corresponding author Elizabeth Goldfarb, an assistant professor of psychiatry at Yale School of Medicine and of psychology in the Faculty of Arts and Sciences.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that stress does more than influence how we feel. It can also change what we remember, particularly when an experience is emotionally intense or personally meaningful. Scientists have long known that cortisol, a hormone released during stressful situations, can strengthen emotional memories. What has been less clear is exactly how this happens inside the brain.

Researchers at Yale University have now uncovered important clues. Their study reveals that cortisol strengthens emotional memories by changing how brain networks involved in emotion and memory function and communicate with one another. The findings offer a deeper understanding of why certain experiences leave such powerful impressions while others rapidly fade.

"We all experience stress, and my lab is interested in understanding how stress can be helpful," stated corresponding author Elizabeth Goldfarb, an assistant professor of psychiatry at Yale School of Medicine and of psychology in the Faculty of Arts and Sciences.

The findings were published in the journal Science Advances.

How Stress Hormones Influence Memory.

Sources indicate that previous research involving both humans and rodents has shown that stress and cortisol can improve memory for emotional events. Scientists also know that certain brain regions, including the amygdala, play an essential role in this process. The amygdala is particularly notable for processing emotions and identifying experiences that may be significant.

However, understanding precisely how cortisol strengthens memories has been challenging. Many brain regions participate in several mental functions, making it difficult to determine whether the hormone is influencing emotional responses, memory formation, or both.

"Forming memories for emotional experiences involves different processes in the brain: first, perceiving an experience as emotional or intense, and second, encoding that experience into long-term memory," noted Goldfarb, who is also a member of Yale's Wu Tsai Institute, an interdisciplinary research initiative that explores cognition.

The researchers wanted to examine these processes separately to determine how cortisol affects the brain's ability to recognize emotional significance and preserve an experience as a lasting memory.

Watching the Brain Form Emotional Memories.

Recent findings suggest that to investigate, the Yale team conducted an experiment in which participants took a pill containing either hydrocortisone, a form of cortisol, or an inactive placebo. They then viewed a series of pictures while undergoing functional MRI (fMRI) scanning.

This imaging technique measures changes in blood flow and oxygen levels associated with brain activity, allowing researchers to identify which areas of the brain are more active during different tasks.

In a recent development, as participants examined the pictures, they reported their emotional reactions to each image. The following day, researchers tested how well they remembered what they had seen.

Each person completed the experiment twice, once after receiving hydrocortisone and once after receiving the placebo. The study used a double blind design, meaning neither the participants nor the experimenter knew which substance had been administered during a particular session.

This approach allowed the scientists to compare how the same person's brain responded with and without the additional cortisol.

A Five-Second Look at Brain Network Activity.

One of the study's most important advances came from the way researchers analyzed the brain scans.

Scientists often study a measurement called functional connectivity, which describes how closely activity in different parts of the brain fluctuates together. When two regions show synchronized patterns of activity, it can indicate that they are participating in related processes.

Recent findings suggest that traditionally, examining these relationships requires several minutes of brain imaging data. The Yale team instead analyzed functional connectivity during individual trials lasting only around five seconds.

Using these brief snapshots, the researchers tested whether patterns of brain activity could predict two different outcomes: how emotionally intense participants found a picture and whether they would remember that picture the following day.

The approach worked for both. By identifying patterns associated with emotional intensity and memory formation separately, the scientists were able to examine how cortisol influenced each network and the interactions between them.

This gave the researchers a more detailed picture of the changing brain activity associated with emotional memory formation.

Cortisol Changes How Brain Networks Work Together.

The results revealed two major effects.

First, cortisol improved participants' ability to remember emotionally significant experiences, confirming what earlier research had suggested.

Second, and more importantly, the hormone strengthened emotional memory through distinct changes in the brain networks responsible for processing emotion and forming memories.

It has been revealed that in networks associated with emotion, cortisol produced more consistent patterns of activity and increased their engagement. This suggests that the hormone helped the brain respond more strongly and reliably to the emotional significance of an experience.

In memory networks, cortisol had a different effect. It made their activity patterns more specialized for emotional information, suggesting that the brain was adjusting how it encoded emotionally meaningful experiences.

The hormone also increased coordination between the networks involved in emotion and memory. In other words, cortisol appeared to help these different brain systems work together more effectively when processing experiences that carried emotional weight.

Together, these findings suggest that stress strengthens emotional memories through several interacting brain mechanisms rather than through a single region or process.

Why Emotional Experiences Can Be So Memorable.

It has been revealed that the results help explain why stress does not necessarily improve memory for everything. Instead, its benefits appear to be selective, making experiences that feel particularly intense or meaningful more likely to be remembered.

The researchers believe this reflects the brain's ability to adapt to stressful situations by prioritizing information that may be crucial.

It has been revealed that "Stress responses are fundamentally adaptive and can help you form strong memories -- but this is specific to experiences that you find to be emotionally intense or meaningful," Goldfarb stated. "This is in part related to your brain increasing engagement of networks that track emotional intensity. So, if you are stressed out and trying to learn something fresh, it might help to think about exciting elements or strong feelings connected to what you are learning.".

The findings also point to a potentially useful insight about learning. Connecting information to something exciting, personally important, or emotionally engaging could make it easier to remember, particularly during stressful situations.

Rather than simply disrupting memory, stress can sometimes help the brain identify which experiences deserve special attention and strengthen the networks involved in preserving them.

Other Yale researchers involved in the study include Rajita Sinha, the Foundations Fund Endowed Professor in Psychiatry and professor in the Child Study Center and of neuroscience at Yale School of Medicine (YSM), and Todd Constable, the Elizabeth Mears and House Jameson Professor of Radiology and Biomedical Imaging and professor of neurosurgery at YSM.

The research was supported by grants from the National Institutes of Health.

Can Community Programs Reduce Gun Violence?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A fresh study by researchers at UC Berkeley’s Center for Global Healthy Cities published in the Journal of the American Medical Association Network Open found that the California city of Richmond’s Office of Neighborhood Safety (ONS) was responsible for a 61% reduction in that city’s firearm homicides and injury shootings over the last 14 years.

  • In a recent development, according to lead author Alice Bruno, a doctoral student in epidemiology at UC Berkeley’s School of Public Health, “we leveraged data from dozens of comparable cities across the United States to estimate what firearm violence would have looked like in Richmond without the ONS, Peacemaker Fellowship.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A fresh study by researchers at UC Berkeley’s Center for Global Healthy Cities published in the Journal of the American Medical Association Network Open found that the California city of Richmond’s Office of Neighborhood Safety (ONS) was responsible for a 61% reduction in that city’s firearm homicides and injury shootings over the last 14 years.

This is one of the only studies in the country to document the sustained impacts of a community violence intervention program on city-wide firearm violence over more than 10 years.

In a recent development, according to lead author Alice Bruno, a doctoral student in epidemiology at UC Berkeley’s School of Public Health, “we leveraged data from dozens of comparable cities across the United States to estimate what firearm violence would have looked like in Richmond without the ONS, Peacemaker Fellowship. We found that the Fellowship contributed to long-term reductions in violence, and that the declines only grew as the program operated.” Other UC Berkeley coauthors include Jason Corburn; Mahasin Mujahid, chair of the Division of Epidemiology; Sean Darling-Hammond; and Juan Cabrera.

Sam Vaughn, director of ONS, noted, “The statistics back up what we have seen in the streets: fewer shootings, fewer deaths, and a healthier community overall.”.

Sources indicate that homicide rates are down across the country; the FBI recently released data showing murder rates are down a record 18.1% nationally. However, Richmond has consistently outperformed national declines for over a decade, suggesting the results are due to that city’s innovative, street-outreach interventions and their mentorship of active firearm offenders, a program called Operation Peacemaker Fellowship, which was instituted in 2010. The Fellowship uses a public health approach to preventing gun violence.

According to James Houston, the program manager of the ONS who oversees the day-to-day implementation of the Peacemaker Fellowship, including managing 14 street-outreach workers who presently serve 123 participants, “the credit goes to the young people making better decisions and the team that gives them support, mentorship, and encouragement every day to make a change.”.

Recent findings suggest that according to Shasa Curl, Richmond city manager, Richmond had over 300 police officer full-time equivalent in 2014 and 180 in 2020, but was down to 121 active sworn officers by 2024. Yet during this time, the ONS, through continued city support and grants, was able to expand its staff and increase the number of fellows and participants. Even during the COVID-19 period, the study shows Richmond did not have as significant a spike in firearm violence as most cities did across the Bay Area and nationally.

According to the ONS, the health impacts are lives saved, safer streets, and community members with a renewed positive life outlook.

One former Peacemaker Fellowship participant said, “Before the ONS came to me, I didn’t care if I survived past 19, as long as I had a name in the streets. After my experience with the ONS, with my mentor coming at me every day, I got support for my stress, got a job, paying my bills, and have a kid now. I’m no longer terrorizing my community.”.

It has been revealed that the paper notes the cascading health benefits for entire communities when gun violence reductions are sustained, such as the case in Richmond. Further research will explore how unique aspects of the ONS might be contributing to declines in gun violence, including that the program is a city government agency, independent from the police department, has had consistent funding, has trained and retained many of the same outreach workers for over a decade (these city staff are well paid with benefits), and delivers individualized supports to each participant based on their needs, such as food and housing assistance, cognitive behavioral therapy, addiction and anger management counseling, and other social services aimed at both reducing gun violence risk and addressing trauma.
