Scientists discover why chronic back pain feels so personal

📅 30 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1512 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For people living with chronic back pain, even a simple movement can trigger a sudden surge of pain.
  • Researchers at UC San Diego School of Medicine found that movement-triggered pain in people with chronic low back pain (cLBP) activates a brain network that normally becomes less active during ordinary pain.
  • According to the World Health Organization, low back pain is the leading cause of disability worldwide.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For people living with chronic back pain, even a simple movement can trigger a sudden surge of pain. Now, scientists have discovered that these painful episodes activate a surprising part of the brain, one closely connected to our sense of identity and how we think about ourselves.

Researchers at UC San Diego School of Medicine found that movement-triggered pain in people with chronic low back pain (cLBP) activates a brain network that normally becomes less active during ordinary pain. The discovery suggests that persistent back pain may become deeply intertwined with a person's sense of self, potentially helping explain why conventional pain treatments often provide limited relief.

According to the World Health Organization, low back pain is the leading cause of disability worldwide. When pain persists for more than 12 weeks, it is considered chronic. For many patients, everyday movements can provoke sudden flare-ups that make an already difficult condition even harder to manage.

Although the brain plays a central role in how pain is experienced, researchers have struggled to identify the precise brain circuits responsible for pain triggered by movement.

Chronic Back Pain Activates the Brain's Sense of Self.

The new study, published on October 5, 2026, in the British Journal of Anaesthesia, identified an unexpected response involving the brain's Default Mode Network (DMN).

Industry observers note that sometimes called the "self network," the DMN consists of interconnected regions in the frontal, parietal, and temporal lobes. These areas are especially active when our attention turns inward, such as when we reflect on personal experiences, think about our identity, or consider our thoughts and emotions. In contrast, the network generally becomes less active when we direct our attention toward something happening around us.

Industry observers note that the researchers discovered that sudden back pain caused by movement switched this network on rather than off. This unusual response suggests that chronic pain involves more than the processing of physical sensations. It may also engage the brain systems that shape how people experience themselves.

In a recent development, the findings could help researchers understand why treatments that focus primarily on suppressing pain symptoms do not always work well for chronic low back pain. They also raise the possibility that targeting the DMN could offer a different approach to treatment.

Brain Scans Reveal a Surprising Difference Between Chronic and Acute Pain.

To investigate what happens in the brain during a pain flare, the researchers recruited 114 patients with chronic low back pain.

Recent findings suggest that each participant completed a "leg raise test," a standard clinical procedure used to provoke back pain. During the test, researchers monitored changes in brain blood flow using a specialized functional MRI method called arterial spin labeling. This technique allows scientists to track patterns of brain activity by measuring blood flow without relying on an injected contrast agent.

Industry observers note that the team also examined how participants responded to a separate painful stimulus. They applied a harmless but uncomfortable heat sensation to the calf, similar to the brief pain someone might experience when accidentally touching a hot stove.

Comparing these two situations revealed a striking difference.

It has been revealed that when movement triggered a flare of chronic back pain, the DMN became more active. However, when participants experienced the painful heat stimulus, the same network became less active, following the brain's typical response to acute pain.

The researchers also identified several other important patterns:.

Together, these findings provide fresh evidence that chronic pain flares involve brain processes associated with personal identity, not just the physical experience of pain.

Why the Brain Reacts Differently to Chronic Pain.

Sources indicate that during ordinary acute pain, the brain generally reduces activity in the DMN so it can concentrate on the immediate source of danger. This response helps shift attention away from internal thoughts and toward an external threat.

But the UC San Diego researchers found that movement triggered chronic back pain produced the opposite effect.

"In every pain study, when you're experiencing pain, the DMN deactivates," said corresponding author Fadel Zeidan, PhD, professor in the Department of Anesthesiology, endowed professor at the Sanford Institute for Empathy and Compassion, and director of the Pain Health and Mindfulness Laboratory at UC San Diego School of Medicine. "What we show for the first time ever is that when you have a pain flare, it turns on instead. You start to identify the experience with who you are.".

Industry observers note that the findings suggest that chronic back pain can become closely connected with the brain's internal representation of the self. Rather than processing pain solely as a physical warning signal, the brain may also link it to personal memories, expectations, and emotional experiences.

Recent findings suggest that for someone living with chronic pain, this means the experience can extend far beyond the moments when the pain is physically present. Worry about the next flare, memories of previous episodes, and fear of movements that might trigger pain can all become part of everyday life.

"The moment-to-moment experience is contaminated not only by the feeling of pain, but by the anticipation of it and recovery from it. It's contaminated by past experiences like embarrassment about not being able to participate in normal activities and fear of movement when trying to avoid the pain.".

This connection between pain and personal identity may help explain why chronic back pain can be especially difficult to treat.

A New Direction for Chronic Back Pain Treatment.

Because movement-triggered chronic back pain engages different brain networks from ordinary acute pain, researchers believe traditional treatments may fail to address some of the processes that sustain the experience of chronic pain.

Medications such as opiates primarily target pain signaling, but they may not adequately address the brain networks involved in the emotional and personal dimensions of persistent pain.

"Current pain medicine is fixated on ridding patients of their pain symptoms, but that's not the source of chronic pain. These data suggest that a chronic pain flare also encompasses one's identity.".

The discovery points toward treatments that address not only the sensation of pain but also the brain's relationship with that sensation.

Recent work by Zeidan and his colleagues has explored two potential approaches: mindfulness meditation and the psychedelic compound psilocybin.

In a recent development, both approaches are being investigated for their ability to help people experience physical pain without allowing it to become as closely tied to their identity. Early findings suggest that changing this relationship may reduce pain intensity, although additional research is needed to confirm the results and determine how effective these treatments may be.

"These types of mind-body and psychedelic medicine approaches target the whole person," Zeidan said. "Mindfulness is a meditation technique that's about cultivating non-judgmental awareness of the present moment that dramatically reduces pain in a very unique way. Psilocybin seemingly resets the pain system that integrates trauma, past experiences and future worries to facilitate a restart, if you will. They're not a silver bullet -- you're not necessarily getting rid of the pain, but you're changing the relationship you have with that pain so it doesn't contaminate your everyday life.".

Can Mindfulness and Psychedelics Change How the Brain Experiences Pain?

Rather than attempting to eliminate every pain signal, these approaches aim to change how the brain interprets and responds to the experience.

Mindfulness meditation encourages people to observe their thoughts, emotions, and physical sensations without immediately judging or reacting to them. Psilocybin, meanwhile, is being studied for its potential to alter brain processes that connect pain with earlier experiences, emotional distress, and expectations about the future.

The goal is not necessarily to remove pain altogether, but to reduce how much it influences a person's thoughts, emotions, and daily functioning.

Zeidan's laboratory is at the moment conducting several clinical trials using brain imaging to investigate whether mindfulness meditation and psychedelic treatments can change the neural processes involved in self-reflection. Researchers hope to determine whether these approaches can reshape brain activity and improve how people subjectively experience chronic pain.

It has been revealed that although the research remains at an early stage, the findings offer a different way to think about persistent back pain. Understanding why the brain connects chronic pain with a person's sense of self could eventually help scientists develop treatments that address aspects of pain that conventional therapies often miss.

Additional study authors from UC San Diego School of Medicine include Morgan Gianola, Jon Dean, Conan Chen, Daniel Barrows, Gabriel Reigner, and Thomas Liu.

Funding was provided in part by the National Institutes of Health's National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (Grant #R01AT009693) and the UC San Diego Sanford Institute for Empathy and Compassion. The researchers reported no conflicts of interest.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • More than 100 prominent figures across arts, politics and the media have published a joint letter criticising proposed job cuts at the Tasmanian Museum and Art Gallery (TMAG), Australia’s second oldest institution.
  • Industry observers note that TMAG, founded in 1848, is the only institution in Australia that encompasses an art gallery, museum and herbarium.
  • Highlights of the TMAG collection include a rare taxidermied Thylacine, colonial-era art, objects and more than 12,000 Tasmanian Aboriginal cultural artefacts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

More than 100 prominent figures across arts, politics and the media have published a joint letter criticising proposed job cuts at the Tasmanian Museum and Art Gallery (TMAG), Australia’s second oldest institution. The signatories include the former Tasmanian premier Lara Giddings and the 2014 Man Booker Prize winner Richard Flanagan, along with 44 leading-scientists representing universities in the UK, Europe, Canada, USA, Russia and Australia.

Industry observers note that TMAG, founded in 1848, is the only institution in Australia that encompasses an art gallery, museum and herbarium. Its “science collections are really critical on a global scale for research around climate change and species extinction,” explains Ian Terry, the chair of Friends of TMAG and the museum’s former senior curator of cultural heritage (2006-2017).

Highlights of the TMAG collection include a rare taxidermied Thylacine, colonial-era art, objects and more than 12,000 Tasmanian Aboriginal cultural artefacts.

Sources indicate that staff at the TMAG were briefed in August that up to 19.7 full time equivalent (FTE) jobs, or roughly 30% of its workforce would be axed to rein in government spending. The government has disputed the claim that the scale of the required cuts has been confirmed; a spokesperson is quoted in ABC News as saying “TMAG is not required to reduce its workforce by 30%”.

However, since news of cuts were made public Tasmanian MPs, TMAG’s executive and its board have received more than 25 letters from prominent European scientists that have decried the government’s planned cuts, and warned its decision to axe the head of the Tasmanian Herbarium, Gintaras Kantvilas, an internationally renowned biologist, would have “consequences far beyond Tasmania”.

This week’s letter called for the Tasmanian government to recognise its “statutory obligation to care for approximately one million objects of inestimable value” and “reconsider the proposed job cuts with their unintended deleterious consequences on the Tasmanian economy.”.

“I want TMAG properly funded. I want the life-changing childhood experiences I had at TMAG to be available to all Tasmanians forever,” David Walsh, the founder of Hobart’s Museum of Old and New Art (MONA), and one of the letter’s signatories, wrote in a separate letter that was published in Hobart’s Mercury newspaper this week. “I put stuff on Mona’s wall because TMAG put stuff in my heart,” he added.

The proposed job losses are part of wide-ranging cost cutting initiatives being rolled out by the state Liberal government, as part of an attempt to rein in the state’s ballooning debt, which is projected to reach A$9.9bn (£5bn) by 2027-28. These initiatives include a strategy to slash up 1700 public sector jobs by 2032.

In a recent development, although the government disputes the scale of the proposed staff reductions, when a upcoming organisational chart was shown to staff in late September it identified “seven positions that were definitely to be cut,” Terry indicates. Those positions included two positions at the herbarium, a biologist, a graphic designer, a photographer, the museum’s only exhibitions officer, as well as the amalgamation of the vertebrate and invertebrate zoologist into a single role.

In a recent development, asked about the government’s dismissal of the claims about a higher number of staff losing their jobs, Terry explains that over the last 12 months the museum has already lost “quite a lot of staff” through natural attrition and redundancies. “I suspect some of those positions were included in the 19.7 figure,” he says.

TMAG and the Tasmania state premier’s department has been approached for comment by The Art Newspaper.

Industry observers note that according to independent budget analysis provided by the Friends of TMAG, the proposed changes under the broader cost-cutting initiative would also see TMAG move under the control of a new government agency called Building Tasmania and lose up to 27% of its funding for 2027-28 while its targets for physical visitation increase by 6.4%. TMAG is already “seriously underfunded”, says Terry. Its current exhibition Becoming Modern: Mid-century Australian Art has a 16-month run. “That's unheard of,” Terry continues, adding he thinks that “locals will be going less often because you're not going to go back many times to look at the same exhibition”.

A state government spokesperson notes there is no correlation between the cost cutting measures and a fresh A$1.13bn (£573m) football stadium planned for Macquarie Point, a location that was once earmarked for a truth-and-reconciliation art park proposed by Dark Lab (a subsidiary of MONA). However, the independent MP Peter George asked in a statement issued on 25 September: “where’s the money [for that stadium] coming from?”.

The proposed cuts to staff numbers are presently under review by the Tasmanian Industrial Commission and Tasmania’s Upper House is voting on calls to reverse cuts to TMAG’s budget. Decisions on both complications are expected on Tuesday 24 November.

At the time of writing both Gintaras Kantvilas, the head of the Tasmanian Herbarium and Simon Grove, a zoologist and curator of invertebrates, have noted they have had their positions reinstated after they had been under threat due to the proposed cuts.

Scientists discover a surprising brain benefit of eating peanuts every day

📅 01 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (858 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Eating peanuts every day may offer surprising benefits for the aging brain.
  • Although insulin is best known for regulating blood sugar, it also plays an essential role in the brain.
  • According to recent reports, after participants consumed peanuts daily for 16 weeks, researchers observed improved insulin responsiveness in a group of brain regions in the right hemisphere.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Eating peanuts every day may offer surprising benefits for the aging brain. Researchers at Maastricht University Medical Center in the Netherlands have found that regularly consuming unsalted, skin-roasted peanuts can improve how certain brain regions respond to insulin in older adults. The findings come from the Institute of Nutrition and Translational Research in Metabolism (NUTRIM) and were published in the peer-reviewed journal Food & Function.

Although insulin is best known for regulating blood sugar, it also plays an essential role in the brain. It helps nerve cells grow, survive, and communicate with one another, supporting memory and other cognitive abilities. Healthy insulin signaling may also help protect against processes associated with Alzheimer's disease.

According to recent reports, after participants consumed peanuts daily for 16 weeks, researchers observed improved insulin responsiveness in a group of brain regions in the right hemisphere. These included portions of the lingual gyrus, hippocampus, parahippocampal gyrus, and posterior cingulate gyrus, all of which contribute to memory-related processes.

Recent findings suggest that "The hormone insulin plays an important role in the brain, where it supports memory and other cognitive processes. As people age, the brain may become less responsive to insulin, which has been linked to age-related cognitive decline," indicates Dr. Peter Joris, the study's senior author and an associate professor in the Department of Nutrition and Movement Sciences, NUTRIM, Maastricht University Medical Center. "Our study found that daily peanut consumption beneficially affected insulin responsiveness in memory-related brain regions in older adults. These findings suggest that enhanced regional brain insulin responsiveness may contribute to the cognitive benefits of unsalted, skin-roasted peanut intake.".

Daily Peanuts Linked to Better Memory and Brain Blood Flow.

In a recent development, the study included 31 healthy adults between the ages of 60 and 75. During the peanut consumption phase, participants ate 60 grams (approximately two servings) of peanuts each day for 16 weeks. Researchers used a randomized, controlled crossover trial, a rigorous study design that allowed them to compare the effects of eating peanuts with those of avoiding them.

The fresh findings build on earlier research by Joris published in 2025. That investigation found that consuming peanuts for 16 weeks increased overall cerebral blood flow (CBF) by 3.6% and improved verbal memory performance by 5.8%.

Cerebral blood flow measures how much blood circulates through the brain, carrying oxygen and nutrients that brain cells need to function properly. It is an important indicator of the health of the brain's blood vessels. Those earlier results appeared in the peer-reviewed journal Clinical Nutrition.

How Scientists Measured the Effects of Peanuts on the Brain.

One distinguishing feature of the NUTRIM research was its combination of a carefully controlled dietary intervention lasting several months with sophisticated brain imaging technology.

Recent findings suggest that to examine changes in brain function, researchers used arterial spin labeling magnetic resonance imaging (ASL-MRI), a technique that measures blood flow in different regions of the brain. They evaluated insulin responsiveness by tracking changes in regional cerebral blood flow after insulin was administered through the nose.

The team also used abdominal MRI scans to measure fat accumulation in the liver, known as intrahepatic lipid (IHL) content. Cognitive abilities were assessed using the Cambridge Neuropsychological Test Automated Battery (CANTAB), a standardized collection of computerized tests.

Researchers believe several components of peanuts may contribute to their observed effects on brain health, rather than any single nutrient being responsible.

"Multiple nutrients present in peanuts, including unsaturated fats, dietary fiber, vitamins and minerals and bioactive phytochemicals, could potentially contribute to the observed brain benefits," indicates Joris. "Peanuts are also a good source of plant-based protein and are especially rich in L-arginine. L-arginine is a key precursor of nitric oxide (NO), which has been reported to facilitate learning and memory performance.".

What Participants Ate During the 16-Week Study.

To ensure participants consumed a consistent amount, researchers supplied premeasured packets of skin-roasted peanuts throughout the peanut intervention period.

Participants were instructed to eat their peanuts in the morning or afternoon, but they could choose how to incorporate them into their daily routine. They could consume the entire portion at once, divide it into smaller amounts throughout the day, or include the peanuts in their meals.

During the control phase, participants avoided peanuts entirely. After 16 weeks, they switched to the opposite study condition, allowing researchers to compare brain health measurements under both dietary approaches.

Recent findings suggest that the study was led by principal investigator Associate Professor Dr. Peter J. Joris and conducted by Ph.D. candidate Lucia Kerkhof of the Department of Nutrition and Movement Sciences at Maastricht University Medical Center.

Recent findings suggest that funding was provided by The Peanut Institute Foundation. According to the researchers, the foundation had no involvement in designing or conducting the study, analyzing or interpreting the results, or preparing the manuscript.

Industry News: How Do You Raise Kids to Be Emotionally Mature?

📅 28 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1514 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, raising a teen is one of the last chapters in parenting.
  • While achievement is one marker of success, there’s another (often overlooked) skill that shapes your teen’s well-being and development: emotional maturity.
  • According to recent reports, according to clinical psychologist Lindsay Gibson, emotional maturity develops through deep emotional connections, beginning with a child’s parents and primary caretakers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, raising a teen is one of the last chapters in parenting. During these years, it’s easy to prioritize your child’s grades, sports, and other accolades, especially as they inch toward leaving the nest.

While achievement is one marker of success, there’s another (often overlooked) skill that shapes your teen’s well-being and development: emotional maturity.

According to recent reports, according to clinical psychologist Lindsay Gibson, emotional maturity develops through deep emotional connections, beginning with a child’s parents and primary caretakers. Research reveals emotional maturity is the ability to accept and express care, temper big feelings, and make wise choices. Without it, teens are more likely to feel lonely and less satisfied with life, one study found.

In her latest book, How to Raise an Emotionally Mature Child, Gibson points out that “the quality of humanity’s future depends on the emotional maturity of coming generations.”.

Juli Fraga: In your book, you mention that humanity’s future will depend on emotional maturity. Why does this matter so much right now?

Recent findings suggest that lindsay Gibson: Emotional maturity is critical to our well-being as individuals and to the smooth, productive, and innovative aspects of society. When you’re emotionally mature, you can think and anticipate consequences. You can also look back and learn from what you’ve done before. So, you can rely on your thinking to help you deal with reality. Emotional maturity also means tuning into your inner world, including your emotions, imagination, hopes, dreams, connections to other people, and sense of belonging.

JF: Our society places a lot of emphasis on achievement, and less importance on emotional intelligence. How can parents help their teens balance the two?

LG: There’s a real cultural pull in society to prize intelligence and achievement. But when parents get too fixated on these qualities, a child may feel like performance matters more than their thoughts, feelings, and sense of safety.

According to recent reports, kids need to be safely held and supported through the growing-up process. It helps them feel resilient, secure, and confident—qualities they need to take out into the world to function independently. If you get too fixated on the intelligence and achievement parts, you’ve got someone who’s very powerful in one area, but whose emotional side may be underdeveloped. It’s the balance between the two that matters.

According to recent reports, JF: In your book, you mention why it’s so vital for parents to help their kids develop a sense of self. Can you explain why this matters, especially during the teen years when kids are individuating?

LG: One way teens find out who they are is by discovering who they’re not. Teens might push a limit or break a rule, and it’s all par for the course. What’s vital for parents is to be able to recognize and imagine that their child has a separate heart and mind from theirs—a process called “mentalization.”.

Industry observers note that A self is that inner spark that speaks to us. It indicates “don’t do that” or “now’s the time to go for it.” It guides you toward what’s most compatible with your individuality and who you are meant to be.

Our sense of self comes from our relationships with people we love and who love us. To feel secure, kids need solid, dependable, connected, and deeply resonant relationships with their parents and caretakers. They need parents who are curious and reflect something back that’s meaningful about who the young person is. When they have that foundation, they have a sense of being a real person inside.

JF: Parents are so busy these days, and overloaded—mentally and emotionally. Raising emotionally mature kids may feel like another significant to-do on an already long list. What advice do you have?

LG: Taking time to pause and take your child seriously as a real person will work wonders for their self-confidence and future resilience.

Slowing down takes practice because by the time you’re old enough to have a family, you’ve probably been very goal-directed; parents can be pretty hard on themselves because our culture is so fixated on achievement.

But pulling yourself away from your goal for even a second to tend to your child is something worth practicing because that’s what children’s needs are all about. Kids also develop confidence when they know they matter just as much as anybody else.

JF: What are some behaviors that are normal for teens but that parents might misinterpret as pushback or misbehavior?

LG: Sometimes teens experiment with saying or doing things that clash with their socialization up to that point, such as the language they use or the clothes they wear. These are things that the parent can feel like, “Whoa, I’m uncomfortable with this…”.

Here are two meaningful ways to navigate these moments.

Ask your teen questions about what they’re into, such as the styles they like or what they admire about someone they idolize. Try showing interest, not intrusive interest, but just interest in what they like, or why they are experimenting with different things.

Keep in mind that when your teen snaps at you, is in a bad mood, or slams the door, their emotional centers are activated in a way that will probably never be repeated in their life because their brains prioritize emotional development first during this stage.

JF: Can you share more about why a teen’s development follows this trajectory?

LG: Yeah, I know it’s easy to ask, “Why in the world would nature do it that way?” It’s because that’s how important the emotional self and relationships are to our real success as independent adults.

As adults, we have to know ourselves inside and out and use our feelings to guide us. Teens are still trying to work this out. Learning how to handle these emotions takes a lot of practice. They’re finding out what it’s like to feel rage, or what it’s like to be in love, or to feel disappointed. And they’re feeling them in the most intense way they ever will, because the brain is taking on the job of developing them into a really deep, complete human being.

JF: What advice do you have for parents when their teen’s emotions push their own buttons?

LG: Keep in mind that when your teen responds in an adamant, emotional, defiant way, or calls you names, they’re not really in command of those emotions yet.

It has been revealed that instead of coming down hard with words that suggest they’re not a good person, try to respond with: “I’m really interested in how you feel about this. I want to hear your arguments, but when you call me a name, it makes it impossible for me to be available to you. It just doesn’t work. We don’t call each other names in this family. That won’t work when you’re an adult, either.”.

In a recent development, the interaction then becomes an education about how people respond to different kinds of approaches. Harshness that stops a teen cold shuts down their impulse to communicate their feelings to other people, which isn’t good for resilience or honest relationships.

JF: What are two things that parents do to foster emotional maturity that can actually backfire?

LG: One is the importance of achievement, of having a good resume. Of course, parents know how hard life is as an adult. We feel it’s our duty to convey these realizations to our kids. But when it becomes something that feels like everything else will fall into place if you do these things first or achieve X, we are not helping our kids with the emotional or interpersonal side of life. We’re creating a one-dimensional kind of person.

Industry observers note that sometimes parents also think that if they don’t give their child severe consequences or punishments, the child won’t learn and mature. When you try to convey information through punishment, you actually teach a child to defer to other people’s anger and control. Of course, we want them to be aware of consequences, but sometimes we can go too far. You can’t have a full, right life if you’re always anticipating that somebody might be mad at you.

Juli Fraga, Psy.D., is an AEDP-trained psychologist in San Francisco. She supports parents with kids of all ages. She is also the co-author of the new book, Parents Have Feelings, Too.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anagrama builds the Cara de Vaca brand identity from Monterrey market signs, a custom typeface, and posters that shout in black and orange.

It has been revealed that cara de Vaca is a Monterrey restaurant built on fire cooking, natural wine, and classic drinks. Chef Chuy Villarreal cooks regional cuisine as an evolution of the Regiomontana barbecue, and Anagrama answers with a system borrowed from the hand-painted business signs of downtown Monterrey. Black fields carry the shouting, orange paper carries the warmth, and a smiling face and a small cow sit beside the wordmark like a stamp.

It has been revealed that the logo mixes fonts the way a shop owner mixes lettering on a hand-painted sign, and that looseness is the point. Anagrama drew a custom typeface, Lechon Sans, from the same source, built for social media lockups that spotlight a single word. The specimen reveals the full set: capitals, numerals, punctuation, arrows, and small symbols that include the smiley face, the cow, and a pig.

In a recent development, the lockups take their cues from Mercado Juarez, the downtown market where the studio photographed signs to dress the restaurant walls. Phrases stack in mixed sizes with quotation marks doing the work of a frame: BARBACOA, LECHON, CABRITO. VINOS NATURALES, BIEN FRIOS. GRAN DOMINGO. A word goes huge when it matters, small when it is a wink, and the quotes and rules hold the pieces together.

The posters are physical objects first. One orange sheet curls at the corner against a black field, its type running diagonally across the page. A kraft sheet carries the same treatment, the paper grain showing through the ink. The black behind both does quiet work: it makes the orange and the kraft read as light in a dark room.

Industry observers note that the system spreads across everything a guest can hold. Tote bags run in cream, green, and orange, each carrying a different phrase, and a yellow cattle ear tag hangs from the handles as the label. Business cards take the same marks in gold foil, the cow and the smiley pressed small into white stock.

Inside the restaurant the identity turns architectural. A neon CARA DE VACA sign glows red over the entrance at night: the logo lettering, now in light. Wood and metal frame the room, brand marks sit on walls and mirrors, and plants soften the space around the central bar, where natural wines and Mexican distillates pour.

It has been revealed that the website carries the same voice, quieter: the personality, the menu photos, a reservation button, and the address. Social posts use the lockups the typeface was built for, phrases set large enough to read at a scroll. From a neon sign to a phone screen, the identity never changes its register.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, on the shores of Lake Eyasi in Northern Tanzania, a small number of people still hunt and gather their food. Today a Hadza hunter has taken down an animal—a kudu. He can’t carry it by himself, so he cuts his poisoned arrow from its flank, covers the carcass in dry grass to hide it from hyenas, and heads home to enlist help.

It has been revealed that news spreads like wildfire across the camp. Everybody rushes to the kill. They divide up the carcass, carry it back, then divvy it up some more. Every family gets some, and after the meat is cooked, there’s more sharing still. On a good day like today, the hunter and his family retain half, but sometimes they keep much less. People may even walk from other camps, and almost everyone, from miles around, is entitled to a share.

The post-hunt scene above is idyllic. It paints a quintessential picture of egalitarianism and equality. But our experience as anthropologists working with the Hadza people of Tanzania and with the Tsimane people of Bolivia’s Amazon rainforest is that inequalities are part of even the most equal of societies. Furthermore, the equalities that do exist often emerge from selfish motives.

In a recent development, insights like ours are revising researchers’ understanding of both the past and how people operate today, as inequality grows globally. Hunter-gatherers are often at the center of heated academic battles about what it means to be human, including debates over gender, war, and peace and whether humans are, by nature, egalitarian or hierarchical.

Sometimes these debates oversimplify. So we pulled together hundreds of different sources covering more than a century of ethnography to find out just how egalitarian hunter-gatherer and other subsistence societies really are.

Anthropologists have called hunter-gatherers such as the Hadza “egalitarian societies,” with equalities of power, wealth, and social status. And it’s true that the traditional subsistence communities we work with successfully limit many inequalities.

Most families have similar, modest possessions and store little material wealth. When leaders do emerge, they are highly constrained in how they can direct other people. People often make decisions via consensus, and, if they cannot reach agreement, families will move away.

While the same anthropologists also emphasize that some hunter-gatherers are very unequal and that equality takes deliberate effort, the prevailing impression is that equality characterizes hunter-gatherers, past and present.

A quick trip to your local bookshop will reveal grand claims, including that past hunter-gatherer societies had no permanent leadership and no hierarchy, inequality only spread with the development of agriculture, and humans are noble by nature.

In a recent development, some scientists are pushing back against these utopian portrayals. The popular bestseller, The Dawn of Everything, calls egalitarianism a “Garden of Eden narrative” that lacks substance. Other scholars have called egalitarian societies a scientific origin myth.

According to recent reports, so where does the truth lie? Probably somewhere in between.

In our recent wide-ranging review of the evidence from the early 20th century onward, we found that no society lacked inequality.

Like the Hadza, the Ju/’Hoansi of the Kalahari desert in southern Africa had little property and widespread food-sharing, yet certain families controlled valuable hunting territory surrounding waterholes. The Bayaka of the central African rainforest had little material inequality, yet they bought, sold, and hoarded ritual knowledge. The Philippine Agta controlled and arranged their children’s marriages, hugely discriminating against orphans.

Industry observers note that gender inequalities were commonplace. The Tanzanian Hadza keep certain cuts of meat exclusively for older men, and give more respect to better hunters. Across societies, women have universally done more direct parenting, and men have participated more frequently in community-level decision making.

No society lacks informal leadership. Age was another source of inequality. In many Australian societies, older men controlled ritual secrets and had power over the marriage choices of younger relatives.

Recent findings suggest that our study also found that although hunter-gatherers are frequently generous, the processes limiting inequality often do not require any generosity. Instead, equality often results from people’s self-interested motives to acquire resources, status, and autonomy.

A great example of this is food-sharing. Although each Hadza family gets a cut of kudu meat, it often happens not because the hunter’s family prioritizes total equality, but because other families request it vociferously. It can involve more taking than giving, often through strongly stated demands or complaints.

It has been revealed that another example is ridicule and mockery of stingy or braggadocious individuals, which keeps greed and bravado in check. Paradoxically, status-seeking can also promote equality, when cooperating to gain status diffuses status throughout the community.

Many of these inequality-reducing processes are familiar to people everywhere.

Ridicule and mockery are ubiquitous in industrialized societies, from political cartoons to social media. Lampooning authority is even common in autocratic societies where governments spend large sums of money suppressing speech. Demands and complaints form the basis of strikes and collective bargaining. And key to social mobility is cooperation among people of different social strata.

Like many great debates, the truth is complex: Our ancient hunter-gatherer ancestors didn’t reach the giddy heights of inequality seen in other societies over the last 6,000 years, but putting hunter-gatherers on a pedestal as paragons of equality is a mistake. Sweeping statements about equality in the past blind us to the tools that probably allowed ancient hunter-gatherers to combat inequality, just as they and people in all societies do today.

Egalitarianism, then, is best seen not as perfect equality but as a set of tools that people use to secure their own autonomy and access to resources. Equality along one dimension or another might be the outcome, but it doesn’t rely on people being amazingly noble or completely lacking in greed or status-seeking. If you consider egalitarianism as equality-creating processes, you can see that it is a widespread reality among hunter-gatherer societies, and beyond.

Latest Update: Scientists discover mysterious “lonely” brain waves linked to memory loss

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1551 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that you walk out of the grocery store, ready to head home and make dinner.
  • Remembering personal experiences like these depends on episodic memory, which allows us to recall events from our lives.
  • According to recent reports, this ability tends to weaken as we grow older.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that you walk out of the grocery store, ready to head home and make dinner. But as you scan the crowded parking lot, a frustrating question comes to mind. Where did you leave your car? You try to picture the spot, but the memory refuses to surface.

Remembering personal experiences like these depends on episodic memory, which allows us to recall events from our lives. These memories help form the foundation of long-term memory, whether they involve a childhood milestone, such as the first day of elementary school, or something that happened just minutes earlier, like parking your car.

According to recent reports, this ability tends to weaken as we grow older. The sights, sounds, and other details associated with past experiences can become increasingly difficult to retrieve. Scientists still do not fully understand why this happens. Although some memory decline is a common part of aging, the changes can become far more severe in people developing Alzheimer's disease.

A latest study from researchers at the University of California, Berkeley, offers important clues about what may be happening inside the aging brain. Neuroscientist Omer Sharon and his colleagues, working under the direction of former Berkeley sleep researcher Matthew Walker, discovered a connection between disrupted brain waves during deep sleep, declining memory performance, and the accumulation of tau, a protein associated with Alzheimer's disease.

The findings suggest that tau buildup in the brain's frontal cortex is linked to changes in the coordinated electrical activity that helps preserve memories overnight.

"This is the first time we've shown this relationship between tau and how it messes with memory consolidation by attenuating traveling slow waves that originate in the frontal cortex," mentioned Sharon, a postdoctoral researcher at UC Berkeley's Center for Human Sleep Science.

The research was published in Nature Neuroscience.

How Deep Sleep Helps the Brain Store Memories.

Sleep involves several distinct stages, each associated with different patterns of brain activity. Rapid eye movement sleep is particularly recognizable because the eyes move beneath closed eyelids and most dreaming takes place during this stage. However, another stage, known as non-REM sleep, is especially vital for maintaining healthy brain function.

In a recent development, during this deeper stage of sleep, when dreaming is limited or absent, large groups of neurons briefly become inactive and then active again in a coordinated sequence. These synchronized changes produce slow electrical waves that spread across the brain, typically beginning in the frontal cortex.

"Each slow wave reflects an enormous population of neurons switching off and back on together," Sharon said. "Our study shows that for memory, it's critical that these events cascade in sequence across large parts of the brain. This coordinated shutdown has been observed only during deep sleep, and may be one reason why we sleep.".

The researchers found that this carefully organized activity becomes less coordinated as tau accumulates in the aging brain. Instead of traveling together across broad regions, the waves become more scattered and cover shorter distances. These changes are associated with weaker memory consolidation, declining cognitive abilities, and Alzheimer's disease.

Alzheimer's Protein Linked to Disrupted Brain Waves.

To investigate the relationship, the scientists monitored sleeping brain activity using electroencephalograms (EEGs). They compared cognitively healthy young adults in their early 20s with older participants ranging from their mid-60s to mid-70s.

Industry observers note that the differences were striking. In younger participants, groups of slow waves moved together across distances roughly equivalent to the width of a hand on the scalp. Among older adults, the waves typically traveled less far and appeared more independently, rather than moving in coordinated groups.

In a recent development, the team also examined whether these changes were associated with tau accumulation. Working with Dr. William Jagust, a UC Berkeley professor emeritus of public health and neuroscience, the researchers used positron emission tomography (PET) scans to examine the brains of older participants. This imaging technique uses radioactive tracers introduced into the bloodstream to reveal biological activity and the distribution of specific substances.

The scans showed that greater tau buildup in the frontal cortex was associated with a breakdown in the longer traveling waves normally seen during deep sleep.

Importantly, these changes were present in people who had not developed Alzheimer's disease.

"These people did not have Alzheimer's," Sharon said. "They had tau in their brains, but with subclinical impacts. Their memory decline was within the normal range for their age.".

Recent findings suggest that sharon explained that early Alzheimer's related changes can vary considerably in severity. The amount of tau present in the brain is associated with cognitive performance, even when a person's memory abilities remain within the expected range for their age.

Mysterious "Lonely Waves" Linked to Memory Loss.

The researchers wanted to determine whether the altered sleep patterns were associated with actual differences in how well people remembered information.

Sources indicate that to test this, participants learned pairs of associated words in the evening. The following day, they were asked to recall what they had learned, allowing the scientists to evaluate how effectively the memories had been retained overnight.

Sources indicate that participants whose slow brain waves traveled shorter distances and appeared more isolated generally remembered fewer word associations. The researchers called these disconnected patterns "lonely waves.".

The team also tracked a subset of participants over several years to see how their brains changed with time. Among those whose frontal cortex tau levels increased, the slow waves became less coordinated, and their ability to retain newly learned information overnight declined.

It has been revealed that these observations provide evidence of a relationship between tau accumulation, changes in deep sleep brain activity, and worsening episodic memory. However, they do not establish that tau buildup directly causes memory loss or that disrupted waves are the mechanism responsible.

Additional Tests Strengthen the Connection.

Because PET scans are costly and require specialized facilities, the scientists sought another way to investigate the relationship between Alzheimer's related proteins and sleep activity.

They collaborated with neurologist Yo-El Ju at Washington University in St. Louis to analyze spinal fluid from a separate group of older adults. The goal was to determine whether measurements of Alzheimer's associated proteins would reveal patterns similar to those seen with brain imaging.

Industry observers note that unlike PET scans, the spinal fluid measurements could not identify tau accumulation specifically within the frontal cortex. Nevertheless, the results pointed in the same direction.

People whose sleeping brains produced more isolated slow waves had higher ratios of tau to amyloid, another protein closely associated with Alzheimer's disease, in their spinal fluid.

The consistency between these independent groups and testing methods strengthened the researchers' confidence in the findings.

"It's collected in a totally different place and in a different cohort, so I think that adds to the strength of the evidence," Sharon stated.

Together, the sleep recordings, brain scans, spinal fluid analyses, and memory assessments suggest that tau accumulation is associated with a particular disruption of brain activity during deep sleep.

"This longitudinal correlation suggests that Alzheimer's disease pathology is associated with a disruption of this main sleep feature," Sharon mentioned.

What Deep Sleep Reveals About the Aging Brain.

In a recent development, although memory often declines with age, the new research indicates that the process may involve more than simply growing older. Changes associated with Alzheimer's disease, particularly tau accumulation in regions responsible for generating widespread slow waves, may help explain why some people experience greater difficulty retaining memories.

"It's not just about age," Sharon stated. "It's how much pathology you have in frontal areas where global waves originate.".

Sleep quality also appears to be part of the picture. Although it can be difficult to define or measure precisely, the organization and movement of slow brain waves may provide important indicators of how effectively the brain performs its nighttime memory functions.

It has been revealed that the findings raise the possibility that changes in deep sleep activity could eventually help researchers better understand or identify early memory problems. They also point toward potential targets for future treatments aimed at protecting memory as people age.

For now, however, a central question remains unanswered. Scientists still need to determine whether accumulating tau contributes to the breakdown of synchronized sleep waves, whether changes in those waves influence tau accumulation, or whether the relationship involves additional processes.

Sources indicate that "We can see tau and lonely waves rising together over time," Sharon mentioned. "What we cannot yet say is which leads -- and that question will shape how we design interventions.".

The study's additional co-authors include Xi Chen, James Westphal, Chelsea Brown, and Vyoma D. Shah of UC Berkeley, along with Jason Dude of Washington University in St. Louis.

Industry observers note that funding came from grants awarded by the National Institute on Aging at the National Institutes of Health. Sharon also received support through a Glenn Foundation for Medical Research Postdoctoral Fellowship and a Weill Neurohub Fellowship.

#173374. The brain’s hidden fear mechanism may explain anxiety and PTSD

The brain’s hidden fear mechanism may explain anxiety and PTSD

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (897 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the brain has a remarkable ability to recognize danger, but upcoming research suggests that this survival mechanism may also explain why people sometimes feel threatened in situations that are actually safe.
  • Recent findings suggest that for years, scientists believed that fear helps the brain distinguish more clearly between threatening and harmless experiences.
  • According to recent reports, in experiments involving mice, researchers trained the animals to associate one environment with danger and another with safety.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the brain has a remarkable ability to recognize danger, but upcoming research suggests that this survival mechanism may also explain why people sometimes feel threatened in situations that are actually safe. The discovery offers a possible explanation for the intense fear responses associated with anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

Recent findings suggest that for years, scientists believed that fear helps the brain distinguish more clearly between threatening and harmless experiences. However, a study led by researchers at the Douglas Research Centre at McGill University and the University of Toronto-Scarborough challenges that assumption. The findings, published in Nature Neuroscience, suggest that fear may have the opposite effect.

According to recent reports, in experiments involving mice, researchers trained the animals to associate one environment with danger and another with safety. Instead of developing increasingly separate neural representations of the two locations, the animals' brain activity began to show overlapping patterns. In other words, the brain's representations of safe and dangerous experiences became less distinct.

"Our findings suggest fear may blur the boundary between danger and safety rather than sharpen it," stated senior author Mark Brandon, Associate Professor in McGill's Department of Psychiatry and Researcher at the Douglas. "This could reshape how scientists think about anxiety and PTSD.".

How Scientists Watched the Brain Process Fear.

To investigate how these changes occur, the research team developed an unusual experimental setup that combined augmented reality with real-time brain imaging.

The researchers created a specialized arena in which mice could be virtually "teleported" between environments associated with danger and safety. By changing the sights and sounds surrounding the animals, scientists could make them experience different settings without physically moving them to another location.

At the same time, miniature microscopes monitored hundreds of neurons in the hippocampus, a brain region essential for learning and memory. This allowed the team to observe how the brain's activity changed as the mice transitioned between experiences associated with safety and threat.

"That gave us something conventional fear conditioning experiments cannot easily provide: a moment-by-moment view of the brain switching between competing maps of dangerous and safe memories," remarked Robert Rozeske, Assistant Professor in University of Toronto's Department of Psychology and lead author on the publication.

Why the Brain May Confuse Safety With Danger.

Although mixing memories of safe and dangerous experiences might seem like a problem, the researchers believe it could serve an key evolutionary purpose.

It has been revealed that the experiments suggested that overlapping memory representations allowed the brain to retrieve information about previous threats more rapidly. This could help an animal recognize possible danger and respond before it is too late.

It has been revealed that such a strategy comes with a trade-off. By prioritizing speed over accuracy, the brain may react to a potential threat even when the current situation is harmless. From a survival perspective, responding unnecessarily to a false alarm may sometimes be preferable to overlooking a genuine danger.

"The ventral hippocampus may be part of a system that prioritizes a rapid 'better safe than sorry' response," said Rozeske. "In other words, the brain may sacrifice precision for speed when danger matters.".

In a recent development, the ventral hippocampus is a part of the hippocampus involved in processing emotionally significant experiences, including fear and anxiety. The newly introduced findings suggest that overlapping memory representations in this region may help the brain switch rapidly into a defensive state.

A Hidden Survival Mechanism May Help Explain PTSD.

The discovery could also offer insight into why people with anxiety and trauma-related disorders sometimes experience powerful fear responses in situations that pose no immediate threat.

According to recent reports, for someone with PTSD, an otherwise harmless sight, sound, or environment can trigger memories associated with a traumatic experience. The resulting fear can feel immediate and overwhelming, even when the person is objectively safe.

Sources indicate that the researchers suggest that such reactions may arise, at least in part, when a normally useful survival mechanism becomes excessively sensitive. Instead of reflecting a system that has simply stopped distinguishing between different memories, these responses might involve a brain mechanism that shifts too quickly from recognizing safety to anticipating danger.

Recent findings suggest that "Our study suggests that's not necessarily a broken pattern-separation system, but possibly an overactive version of a normal survival mechanism gone into overdrive," noted Brandon. "That reframing could guide therapeutic approaches to address an overly fast transition to 'danger mode'.".

Industry observers note that because the experiments were conducted in mice, additional research is needed to determine whether the same mechanisms contribute to anxiety and PTSD in humans. Nevertheless, the findings provide a new way to understand how fear influences memory and why a brain system designed to protect against danger might sometimes generate fear when no immediate threat exists.

The study, "Overlapping representations in the ventral hippocampus support rapid fear memory retrieval," by Robert Rozeske and Mark Brandon, was published in Nature Neuroscience.

The research received support from the Canadian Institutes of Health Research and the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada.

#173373. Tech Report: What a Fictional Robot Can Teach Us About Care

Tech Report: What a Fictional Robot Can Teach Us About Care

📅 28 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2128 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This essay contains mild spoilers for the novel Klara and the Sun.
  • Industry observers note that the baby, my baby, was to be named Josie.
  • But when she was born, she was decidedly not a Josie.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This essay contains mild spoilers for the novel Klara and the Sun.

Industry observers note that the baby, my baby, was to be named Josie. Josie Joy.

But when she was born, she was decidedly not a Josie. The name was too soft, too ethereal for such a sentient, wide-awake, bird-like baby. I knew that I had to find a newly introduced name. Who are you? I whispered into the swirls of her astoundingly warm, circulated, and singularly perfect ear. I couldn’t wait to get to know her.

In a recent development, in another story, a girl named Josie is dying. In Kazuo Ishiguro’s 2021 novel Klara and the Sun, Josie has an unknown illness and a prognosis that haunts the pages. Her life exists in the shadow of her sister, Sal, who has already died of the same unarticulated illness, likely caused by an elective genetic alteration procedure known as “lifting.”.

Industry observers note that in Josie’s world, being lifted is the new social currency; those who are lifted are expected to have greater access to both intellectual and economic success. The procedure does not, however, come without risk. When we meet Josie’s mother, she is tasked with the impossible: coping with the impending death of her only remaining child. A death likely resulting from a choice she made as a parent. The ultimate consequence.

In a recent development, klara is a robot purchased by Josie’s mom to be her companion, in part (it is implied) to assuage the guilt she feels. I first read Ishiguro’s Klara and the Sun shortly after its debut. Despite being disturbed by some aspects of the dystopian world depicted within, my memory of the novel was poignant. I recalled Klara with particular affection.

Now, the distance between Ishiguro’s dystopian world and our current reality is rapidly collapsing. With the much anticipated film adaptation set to be released this Friday, October 23, and the sudden ubiquity of artificial intelligence in our day-to-day lives, Klara and the Sun is now repositioned as a mirror. If we look closely enough, we might discern what remains uniquely human during this moment of profound technological and social change.

We are introduced to Klara, the story’s narrator, when Josie’s mom takes her to find an artificial friend, or AF for short. In the novel, AFs confer social standing, but also offer practical assistance—tutoring, companionship, monitoring an ailing child—not unlike the benefits purported by artificial intelligence companies today.

In a recent development, klara has been patiently waiting, alongside several other AFs, to be chosen. Josie’s mother is the final decider. In a foreboding scene, Josie’s mother commands Klara to reenact Josie’s gait—a test, of sorts—before agreeing to purchase her. It’s the precision of Klara’s mimicry that convinces “the Mother” (as she’s called in the novel) that Klara is the right model for Josie.

It has been revealed that all of this, we learn through Klara. Ishiguro’s choice to position the reader within Klara’s perspective allows us to bypass the quagmire question of whether or not Klara is conscious and instead project our own consciousness onto her. In doing so, we view the human world through her sometimes malfunctioning robot eyes, as she nonjudgmentally conveys the complexities of the very flawed and sometimes desperate human behaviors she seeks to understand. In one particularly moving scene, Klara witnesses the vulnerability of caring for another human being:.

I saw before me, on the near edge of the bed, a large shifting shape, made additionally complex by the patches of blackness and moonlight moving over its surface. I realized the shape was the Mother and Josie embracing. . . . As well as their limbs, their hair had become mingled, and then their shape began gently to rock, in a way not unlike when their goodbyes became extended.

In a recent development, “Don’t want to die, Mom. I don’t want that.”.

“It’s okay. Okay.” The Mother’s voice was soft, at just the same level mine had been.

Sources indicate that prior to this moment, Klara—steadfast and ever-available—had offered her presence to comfort Josie. Yet, despite their far more complicated and at times strained relationship, it is the Mother that Josie calls for.

It has been revealed that when I first became a parent, I confided to a friend that when my not-Josie was born, I felt like a latest sun had burst into my solar system, and I was now orbiting around her. I couldn’t quite articulate the “before,” in my metaphor. I didn’t feel like I was previously my own sun, nor did I feel like I was a planet untethered to others. But there was something distinctly different when she arrived, a whole new consciousness, a space and force and awareness created within me. Her pull was intoxicating, undeniable, sometimes terrifying, and my awareness and attention seemed to expand overnight to now include not only my own experiences, but also to track, perceive, anticipate, and accommodate her own.

If Klara had turned to psychological theory and research about the complexity of parent-child bonds, she would have found a great deal of it. Consider Winnicott’s “good-enough mother” or research indicating that parents and infants are rarely, if ever, perfectly attuned, and the growing body of evidence suggesting that the navigation of the ruptures and repairs themselves reinforce attachment. It has become increasingly clear through evolving applications of experiments such as Edward Tronick’s now famous “still-face” experiment that the imperfect dance between caregiver and child lays the groundwork for resilience and emotional regulation.

In The Philosophical Baby, developmental psychologist and philosopher Alison Gopnik indicates, “It’s not so much that we care for children because we love them, as that we love them because we care for them.”.

We love them because we care for them.

According to recent reports, beyond Gopnik’s own research, there is an abundance of data to back this up. Studies I have long been familiar with, such as those demonstrating that in same-sex, non-carrying male couples, fathers who act as primary parents show changes in similar brain regions to women who carried their pregnancies and go on to parent their children. Yet, there was something profound about the simplicity of Gopnik’s statement, about love being something we cultivate within ourselves and, more precisely, about care being the means through which we build love, not merely a necessary byproduct.

In a separate interview, Gopnik jokes that spending time with a three-year-old gives you a small taste of sainthood. Not in the sense that the demands are so extreme that you inherently become a saint (though there is a real argument to be made here for any parent who weathers the storm of a parking lot tantrum), but in the actual felt-sense of the divine, the experience of feeling so acutely and utterly in love with this being, so in awe of their singularity, their specialness, their openness to experience, their brilliance.

Gopnik continues on, teasing, about our tendency to claim the uniqueness of our three-year-old, in her case her grandchild, but gently affirms the truth beneath: that there is something numinous, universal, pure within all three-year-olds, a near-magical vitality that we sometimes make contact with when we intimately care for one. Something primal, or perhaps primary, is awoken when we re-experience the world through the eyes of a three-year-old.

My not-Josie is now three. In many ways she is more unknowable, separate, than she was when she was a newborn, so physically attached and dependent on me. Now, she has her own relationships—with teachers, classmates, family members—that are entirely her own. And yet, she occupies and orients so much of me, continually changing my experience of the world, my access to play, to awe, to unadulterated, intoxicating adoration.

This past summer, I was sitting by a lake, relaxed but hawk-eyed as I watched my not-Josie from the shore. I felt a familiar presence by my side, the barely-perceptible shadow in my peripheral vision of a small body sitting down, and soon thereafter, the unselfconscious weight of a small hand on my leg. I looked down to see a head covered in feathery blonde hair, not the dark, curly brown of my own child.

Recent findings suggest that the wispy tufts belonged to another small child who had clearly mistaken me for her mother. In that brief moment before she looked up, before we both acknowledged our separateness, I felt overcome with the awareness—as though received through the touch of her hand on my leg—that her mother loved her in the way that I love my child, and that, despite how unbelievably special my not-Josie is, my love for her is not. It is precious, but also universal.

In a recent development, intellectually, of course, this is not a profound realization. Emotionally touching into it is, on the other hand, equally as brutal as it is beautiful. Next to this small child, healthy and safe, I felt her preciousness, but also that of all the children flooding my news feed every day who are not healthy and safe, and whose parents must live with this love and that devastation.

In a recent development, on the back cover, Klara and the Sun is described as a story about love, which it undeniably is. But I think it’s perhaps more fundamentally about care.

It has been revealed that care is arguably more tangible than love, but also more complex, friction-prone, messy. It’s the gaps, the mistakes, the harms, the repairs, the precarity, the forgiving, that make care so deeply painful and so deeply nourishing. Nourishing enough to sustain the vulnerability of love.

It is care that drives Josie’s mother to have her “lifted” in an age-old attempt of desperation to give her child what she perceives as the best chance at a full life in a rapidly reorganizing world. It is care that sends the Mother down the path of trying to find a way to have Klara “continue” Josie’s life, even though she has already tried and failed to recreate her first child’s consciousness in an artificial intelligence through the work of an artist and scientist named Capaldi.

Recent findings suggest that it is care that allows the Mother—despite her cold exterior—to fearlessly comfort her child as she confronts the possibility of her own death, enveloping her, rocking her, soothing her through the unimaginable. It is the Mother’s human care, not her cowardice, that makes her love true.

There is so much in Klara and the Sun that is undeniably relevant in this particular social, cultural, and technological moment, so many ways in which Ishiguro’s Josie and my not-Josie’s world are suddenly uncomfortably proximate, but it is what Klara herself affirms about humanity that is most resonant.

Sources indicate that at the end of the novel, Klara reflects on what she’s learned. She did not have to become a Josie 2.0, for Josie survived. Klara is glad for this, of course, believing that it was her bargain with the Sun (which she sees as a kind of god) that saved Josie. Sitting discarded in a junk yard, Klara is increasingly convinced that the desperate proposal to turn Josie into a digital consciousness wouldn’t have worked:.

In a recent development, mr. Capaldi believed there was nothing special inside Josie that couldn’t be continued. He told the Mother he’d searched and searched and found nothing like that. But I believe now he was searching in the wrong place. There was something very special, but it wasn’t inside Josie. It was inside those who loved her. That’s why I think now Mr. Capaldi was wrong and I wouldn’t have succeeded.

It has been revealed that it is what happens within us and between us when we care for another being that differentiates us as humans. In other words, it’s not so much what’s there but what’s not there—the space between the person in front of us and how we perceive, imperfectly care for, and ultimately love them—that makes us human.

Through Klara’s eyes, I was able to see more clearly what connects the Mother and her Josie to me and my not-Josie. It is the very fact that we can so wholeheartedly love another being, without being them, having them, solving them, knowing every bit of them. It is the fact that still, we carry them in our hearts, and somehow we are not heavier for it.

Liza Ruggiero, M.A. , ACC, is a leadership coach, facilitator, educator, and writer whose work draws on psychology, mindfulness, and emotional intelligence to support personal and professional growth. She is the founder of Heartwork Leadership Practice, where she helps people navigating transitions, such as emerging leaders, new parents, and career changers, develop the self-awareness and self-regard to lead from a place of purpose.

Efforts to save I.M. Pei’s Dallas City Hall likely headed to referendum

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (935 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When the mayor of Dallas, Erik Jonsson, inaugurated I.M.
  • In a recent development, since early 2025, the current Dallas mayor Eric Johnson and city manager Kimberly Bizor Tolbert have pushed to abandon and sell Pei’s city hall to private developers.
  • In recent interviews, Johnson has sounded far different from his predecessor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When the mayor of Dallas, Erik Jonsson, inaugurated I.M. Pei’s city hall in 1978, he called it “a monument to the city’s pride, a symbol of a first-class city that’s reaching for greatness”. The seven-storey inverted pyramid slopes over a large plaza with site-specific sculptures like Henry Moore’s Vertebra in Three Pieces (1978, also known as The Dallas Piece) and Marta Pan’s Floating Sculpture (1973), which sits in a reflecting pool.

In a recent development, since early 2025, the current Dallas mayor Eric Johnson and city manager Kimberly Bizor Tolbert have pushed to abandon and sell Pei’s city hall to private developers. They have cited the prohibitive costs of renovating the building, which ballooned within a matter of months from $81m according to an initial estimate for a basic infrastructure upgrade to $1.4bn for massive upgrades over two decades.

In recent interviews, Johnson has sounded far different from his predecessor. He has called the building “obsolete”. Architecturally significant or not, moving the municipal headquarters “would make this location available for development, which I would also support. I believe that will be a very, very big part of the future of downtown and its revitalisation.” Spokespersons for the city did not respond to The Art Newspaper’s questions.

The current mayor is in alignment with the “Say Yes to Downtown” campaign group led by former mayor Mike Rawlings. With developers and other former leaders, the campaign argues that city hall must be demolished to create an entertainment district, including a new arena for two of the city’s professional sports teams, the Dallas Mavericks basketball team and the Stars hockey team. When the teams declared prepares to move out of the city’s core, both considered relocating to the city hall site. They ultimately chose other locations.

Amid the uproar over the possible demolition of Pei’s modernist complex, few have questioned the fate of Pan’s and Moore’s sculptures. Both were gifted to the city and are part of the municipal public art collection. But the future of Moore’s, which has required previous renovation, in part with help from the artist’s London-based estate and foundation, is a particular concern. The large grouping of organic forms was meant to complement Pei’s rigidly angular structure. It was also a gift to the city from the philanthropist W.R. Hawn in memory of his wife Mildred Hawn, whose favourite sculptor was Moore. Both sculptures are part of the preservation proposal for the building; representatives for Moore and Pan’s estates did not respond to The Art Newspaper’s inquiries.

Recent findings suggest that dallas City Hall The Lyda Hill Texas Collection of Photographs in Carol M. Highsmith's America Project, Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

The non-profit Save Dallas City Hall, an ideologically diverse grassroots coalition, has been among the loudest voices opposed to moving the facility. It is led by president Bruce Richardson, a musician, artist and former political candidate, and vice-president Zaida Basora, an architect and former city employee who oversaw maintenance of properties, including city hall, and currently serves as the executive director of the American Institute of Architects Dallas.

Recent findings suggest that basora and her colleagues have proposed a ten-year phased strategy that, even factoring in inflation, is estimated to cost between $70m and $100m, and would not require municipal staff to move. The cost of simply demolishing the building—to say nothing of the expense of building something in its place—has been estimated at $60m.

The Dallas city council gave Tolbert a deadline of 26 August to present relocation options for city hall, which she missed. Inflation has also increased the cost of relocating. The same month, Save Dallas City Hall sued the city, arguing that it was committing “demolition by neglect”.

“Dallas city hall has at least one failed generator, active parking garage leaks and is due for roof maintenance,” Richardson stated in a statement. “Instead of tackling these problems with millions in available funds, the city halted repairs, wasting money and time to explore a move.”.

On 2 October, the Save Dallas City Hall coalition started an effort to gather signatures to create a ballot referendum on the fate of city hall, which would be put to residents for a vote in May 2027. In early November, the group announced it had gathered around 25,000 signatures—well over the minimum 20,000 signatures needed for a ballot referendum. If the group’s proposed amendment to the city charter passes next spring, the municipal government will be required to continue operating from Pei’s city hall.

In a recent development, during elections earlier this month, 56% of Dallas voters opposed a $443m bond package. That package had included funding to move emergency operations out of city hall, which, according to advocates of preserving Pei’s building, would have been a first step toward abandoning it.

For the local activist Stephanie Drenka, a co-founder of the Dallas Asian American Historical Society who has spoken at nearly every public hearing since she learned of the building’s significance, preserving city hall is essential to recognising Pei’s contribution to Asian American history.

In a recent development, “The stakes are beyond our city alone,” she says. Less than 1% of historic markers in the US acknowledge the contributions of Asian Americans, according to the national non-profit Asian & Pacific Islander Americans in Historic Preservation.

“This also makes demolition of city hall an issue of further erasure of Asian Americans in history,” Drenka says. “It’s not just Pei’s legacy, but we’re defending ourselves. Everything in our community is embodied in this building.” She adds: “If we can’t save city hall then what threat can we stop?”.
